#188489. Latest Update: 90% of employers reject resumes that look like AI – yet half use AI to interview

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1065 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: 90% of employers reject resumes that look like AI – yet half use AI to interview

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider.
  • Newly introduced data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.
  • Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider. At the same time, they’re turning to AI to help screen more candidates — meaning those videos you’ve seen on the internet of people pranking AI interviewers aren’t going away anytime soon.

Newly introduced data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost.

“The survey data is self-reported, so it reflects what employers believe has happened, not a measured outcome,” Greenhouse’s Head of Voice AI Ophir Samson told ZDNET via email.

Sources indicate that employers are also reacting to AI by adjusting their hiring processes: 86% of those surveyed reported changes to account for AI’s impact. 57% of them did so by adding another human interview.

In a recent development, “As jobseekers rely more on AI to polish and send out their job applications, employers are finding it harder to tell who’s actually right for the role,” the report stated, echoing an ongoing push-and-pull between applicants and hiring teams. AI resume screeners automatically toss a majority of applications they deem unfit, so applicants try not to get tossed by formatting their material for the screener, which then backfires anyway.

Recent findings suggest that the report shows how a tough economy and an influx of AI hiring tools are colliding, arguably to benefit employers over applicants. Greenhouse noted that, ironically, AI tools are helping hiring managers while also making resumes untrustworthy, and applicants would rather be interviewed by AI than not at all.

Also: How to beat the AI algorithm and get the job of your dreams.

“A growing number of employers are using AI not just to filter candidates out, but to have conversations with more candidates, earlier, through AI-powered voice technology,” Greenhouse noted, adding that “half now use AI interviews to hear from more candidates, and 40% of those have found strong candidates they would have missed.”.

Greenhouse itself offers a voice AI screening interview tool. Samson told ZDNET that an HR professional ran 200 candidates she’d rejected through Greenhouse’s tool, and it suggested 19.

“All five of the finalists came from that group, and she ultimately hired one from the group,” Samson stated.

Sources indicate that what we don’t, and maybe can’t, know is the inverse: whether AI screeners influence hiring managers to turn away candidates they actually should have considered. At least in Greenhouse’s case, Samson mentioned Voice AI doesn’t make hiring decisions or “automatically advance, reject, or rank candidates.”.

“Recruiters review every output, and one recruiter owns the outcome and can explain how they reached it,” he said.

Greenhouse’s report surveyed 1,347 hiring managers and recruiters across the US, UK, Germany, Australia, and Ireland from late September to mid-October, and found that half of employers using voice AI “say the early-stage candidate experience has improved.”.

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ latest top stressor.

It’s unclear what “improved” means there, though, and whether applicants themselves would agree with that. Still, when given the choice, only 7% of applicants in the US would turn down an AI interview, per an earlier Greenhouse report. Additionally, “70% of those who’ve had a live AI interview say it helped them show their skills,” that report mentioned.

In a recent development, but how swayed is that by the state of the US job market? October’s job report was better than expected, but it’s still been a tough year overall for job-seekers. Greenhouse’s findings could be as much a reflection of how desperate applicants are as an endorsement of or comfort with AI screenings.

“The job market could be a factor. Our Future of Hiring Candidate Report shows 81% of job seekers were rejected from a job in the past year without speaking to anyone at the company, human or AI,” Samson remarked. “But I’d be careful about reading the data as desperation. Candidates are setting clear conditions: nearly half (49%) want to know if a human will review their responses and 40% want to know how they’ll be evaluated.”.

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires – and 5 ways smart leaders generate real value instead.

Samson said that a software engineer named Ryan Quinlan, who was hired at Blissway, initially thought “talking to an AI” sounded stranger, but that it ultimately “felt like a conversation” that let him mention skills he’d forgotten to include on his resume. Samson said that Ryan has been “a ‘maybe’ on paper,” but that the AI interview helped him get over the line to be considered.

In a recent development, “For most applicants, a human conversation was never on the table,” Samson said. “The real choice is a resume lost in a pile, or 15 minutes to tell their story.”.

Greenhouse found that while employers are using AI to screen more candidates, most are maintaining human oversight over the most important decisions in the hiring process.

“Of all the tasks employers would hand to an AI agent, deciding which candidates to advance came last, at just 7%,” Greenhouse said.

A recent California law aims to protect employees from being fired by AI systems that make determinations about their performance without a human co-signing the assessment. As with many AI productivity tools in the workplace, proper adoption ideally equates to more time for human workers to handle more important tasks.

Also: 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside.

“Of employers who’ve saved time with AI, 85% put it back into candidates, most often by spending more time with shortlisted candidates (45%) and interviewing more candidates earlier (40%),” Greenhouse noted.

The main question around AI interviewers remains whether they’re correctly capturing your interview the way you’d hope a human interviewer would (though that’s still deeply subjective and out of applicants’ control anyway).

“When AI interviews are implemented thoughtfully and transparently, they pay off for both candidates and recruiters,” Samson mentioned. “Every candidate who uses our Voice AI can opt out, and about 90% rate the experience as excellent.”.

I Put Xiaomi’s 18 Pro Max Camera to the Test and I Love the Results

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, xiaomi has taken the wraps off its latest 18 Pro Max Android phone in Paris.
  • The images seen here are taken with the phone’s various built-in camera modes, largely the black and white mode, as I love the dramatic, filmic look it produces.
  • Taken using one of the phone’s built-in color styles, I love the vibrancy in this shot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, xiaomi has taken the wraps off its latest 18 Pro Max Android phone in Paris. I’ve had the phone for the past few weeks and have been putting the camera to the test in my beautiful home of Edinburgh, Scotland, as well as on the beautiful (and rainy) streets of Paris. You can check out my review of the phone if you’re keen to hear more about that wild rear screen on the back, but here I wanted to share some of my favorite photos I’ve taken with the phone so far.

The images seen here are taken with the phone’s various built-in camera modes, largely the black and white mode, as I love the dramatic, filmic look it produces. They’re presented either as-shot or with minimal adjustments using the phone’s built-in editing tools.

Taken using one of the phone’s built-in color styles, I love the vibrancy in this shot. The reds really pop, while the wider angle of the main camera emphasizes the tunnel effect of the alleyway, drawing the eye to the person and their dog.

I may be spoiling the rest of the images here by saying that this is my absolute favorite shot I’ve taken, but there we go. I took this using one of the dedicated black-and-white modes, and I think the tones here are perfect. Excellent dynamic range and contrast, and just the right amount of film grain. I positioned the figure between the buildings and had the phone almost on the floor to turn the rain-soaked tiles into a reflective surface to add some drama to this scene. I then applied a wide cinematic crop in post to give it that extra edge. Lovely stuff.

Most of my favorite photos with the phone were taken using the black-and-white mode. It’s no surprise; I shoot in black and white very often on my Leica Q3 43, and I used the monochrome mode for my favorite shots with Xiaomi’s Leitzphone earlier in the year.

The phone captures excellent black-and-white photos at night, too.

And by exposing for the bright highlights in this scene, I was able to create this stark, moody image of my handsome orange cat, Toulouse. Is he the best cat you’ve ever seen? Of course he is.

Back in color, this UFO that had presumably crash-landed in this Parisian market looks great in this filmic color mode. The oranges and reds pop against the other tones in this scene.

While this quick street portrait is similarly punchy.

Industry observers note that I used manual mode here, taking full control over the white balance and exposure settings to achieve the tones I wanted. It’s a great-looking shot with excellent dynamic range. Xiaomi’s phone doesn’t appear to go too hard with its software processing either, meaning that even fine details look quite natural. Other Android phone-makers could take note.

It has been revealed that as with the photo of Toulouse the cat, I exposed for the highlights here, forcing the rest of the scene under this bridge into shadow. As a result, it looks moody and dramatic but crucially it also looks exactly as I hoped it would. Many phones would try to artificially lift the shadows here, which would ruin the vibe I was going for.

Sources indicate that I took this with the phone’s telephoto zoom lens, aiming to focus more on the digger as the subject and use the water for reflection. I love how this shot looks, especially in black and white, as the cloud detail behind it is especially noticeable.

While here I used the full wide angle of the main camera in order to create a lot of negative space around the figures, emphasizing the size of the building around them.

That building was Le Grande Arche in Paris and despite it being a miserably cold, wet and cloudy day I think the phone has captured a satisfyingly stark scene here.

I don’t like flying, so I distracted myself on the flight out to Paris by taking photos of things with the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, including this man having a look out of the window.

It has been revealed that and this shot of my plane’s wing somewhere above the UK. Again, in black and white. When it looks this good, why would I choose anything else?

According to recent reports, and while we’re still in black and white, a particularly friendly pigeon. Hi, friend!

And to round us off, this dude in shades looking at a menu.

Sources indicate that I’m genuinely really thrilled with so many of the shots I’ve taken with this phone. The black-and-white mode in particular is spectacular, and I’m looking forward to taking more shots with it over the coming weeks and months.

Editors’ note: Andrew Lanxon’s travel costs to attend Xiaomi’s launch event in Paris were covered by Xiaomi. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

ESR Black Friday gift guide: Premium accessories for iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, iPad, AirPods, and Apple Watch

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you picked up a latest iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo this fall, or you’re shopping for someone with an iPad, AirPods, or Apple Watch, there’s a good chance you’ve been holding out on purchasing accessories until all of the Black Friday deals started.
  • Sources indicate that ESR has been making Apple accessories since 2009, and that track record has made it a trustworthy name for the more than 123 million people who use its products to protect their Apple devices and make them more versatile.
  • If someone on your shopping list picked up an iPhone Duo, a case is the first thing they need, and it’s also the hardest one to get right.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you picked up a latest iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo this fall, or you’re shopping for someone with an iPad, AirPods, or Apple Watch, there’s a good chance you’ve been holding out on purchasing accessories until all of the Black Friday deals started. We’ve got you covered with some great deals on premium accessories for nearly every Apple device on your list.

Sources indicate that ESR has been making Apple accessories since 2009, and that track record has made it a trustworthy name for the more than 123 million people who use its products to protect their Apple devices and make them more versatile. Here’s a look at what’s included in ESR’s Black Friday lineup and who each one is for.

If someone on your shopping list picked up an iPhone Duo, a case is the first thing they need, and it’s also the hardest one to get right. As we’ve seen with Android foldables, you’re protecting two halves, a hinge, and a phone that changes shape throughout the day as you use it, all without adding bulk to a device people bought because it folds thin. ESR has two options for iPhone Duo owners, and the choice mostly comes down to the look you want to achieve.

The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand is your choice if you want to show off your iPhone Duo’s colors. It combines a rigid polycarbonate and acrylic back with a softer TPU frame. The rigid back keeps the case from flexing and lets the iPhone Duo’s design show through, while the flexible frame absorbs the shock if you drop it (please don’t).

The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand is perfect for those who want a more premium look for their iPhone Duo. It’s made from organic silicone leather with a soft, skin-friendly feel and a stain-resistant finish. If you’ve ever used a light-colored leather case before, you know it usually shows every stain and smudge it comes across, but ESR built the Atelier to resist daily wear and wipe clean.

Both cases share ESR’s Flex Stand, and it’s one of the most innovative and versatile parts of the lineup. It’s a 180-degree rotating stand made from zinc alloy, so it holds its shape even after months of propping up your iPhone. A precision hinge with damping control lets it open smoothly and lock at the angle you choose, whether the iPhone Duo is folded or unfolded, and ESR says it has passed 3,000 open-and-close tests. In real life, that means propping the iPhone Duo open on a desk for a video call or on an airplane tray table for a movie, then using the stand as a grip when you’re holding it.

Both cases add extra hinge protection and raised edges where a foldable is most exposed. If you follow our MagSafe Monday column, you know magnetic strength really matters for MagSafe wallets, car mounts, etc. The Classic Hybrid has 1,500g of magnetic hold, and the Atelier has 1,400g.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case for iPhone Duo is 15% off.

It has been revealed that the same two incredible cases come in iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max versions, and they also fit the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max. The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand has a clear back, a TPU frame, and a PU anti-yellowing coating. In simple terms, TPU is the flexible, shock-absorbing plastic used in most case frames, and it’s also what usually turns clear cases slightly yellow the longer you use them, so ESR adds a polyurethane (PU) coating to shield it. ESR upgraded the case’s UV protection for longer-lasting resistance to yellowing, and it’s SGS-certified for anti-yellowing. A clear case is supposed to show off your iPhone’s color, so staying clear longer is the whole point. The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand retains the same soft silicone leather and stain-resistant finish as the iPhone Duo version.

On these models, the Flex Stand adjusts from 15 to 69 degrees for portrait and landscape viewing. That has you covered for StandBy mode on your nightstand and a show over your lunch break, with no separate stand to carry around.

Protection is where the two cases differ. ESR rates the Classic Hybrid for 4x military-grade protection with 16-foot drop protection, plus a full-coverage camera bar. The Atelier is rated for 3x military-grade protection, including 12-foot drop protection, and features a soft microfiber lining. Military-grade refers to the MIL-STD-810 drop test, which uses a 4-foot drop, so 4x and 3x mean ESR rates the cases for four and three times that height. Both include a built-in Camera Control cover and raised edges, and both use a precise magnetic ring layout that automatically aligns with MagSafe chargers, car mounts, wallets, and batteries.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case is up to 28% off, and the ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case is up to 37% off.

It has been revealed that A case protects everything except the part you touch all day. The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector covers the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, and the name is worth unpacking. Armorite is ESR’s line of toughened screen protectors, and the Pro version is made with Accessory Glass by Corning™. Corning has made the durable glass in Apple products since the very first iPhone, so in non-tech speak, this is glass from a trustworthy name rather than generic tempered glass.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: ESR says the protector delivers 10x the impact absorption of generic protectors, and Corning’s lab testing shows up to 2x better scratch performance and up to 25% less scratch visibility for its Accessory Glass. When you drop your iPhone or toss it in a pocket with your keys, the protector takes the hit instead of your screen. An anti-reflective coating reduces light reflection to just 2.3% while maintaining 94% optical transmittance, resulting in less glare outside and truer color. Edge-to-edge coverage leaves no gaps for dust to collect.

Sources indicate that installation is the part most people dread on a brand-new iPhone, and ESR’s UltraFit tray handles it in two steps. Pull the tab, and the tray’s design clears dust and pushes out air bubbles as the glass goes down. Long gone are the days when you needed “professional installation” for a screen protector to look great.

Black Friday deal: The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector is 15% off.

Holiday travel usually means one open outlet, an iPhone, a laptop, an e-reader, etc., that all need power, and cables left at home. The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger builds the cable in. It has a braided cable that extends to 3.1 feet and fully retracts into the charger, and ESR rates it for 20,000 pulls and 10,000 bends. An extra USB-C port lets a second device charge simultaneously. 9to5Mac’s Michael Burkhardt went hands-on with the Xtend 45W earlier this month and mentioned it’s an excellent iPhone fast charger on the go.

In a recent development, it’s rated at 45 watts and delivers up to 60 watts of dynamic power, enough to fast-charge phones and laptops, and it works with iPhone Duo, iPhone 15 through 18, and Android phones like Galaxy and Pixel. It supports PD 3.2 AVS, which in plain English means the charger and your device talk to each other, and the charger fine-tunes the power it sends to exactly what that device asks for. ESR indicates it can charge an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max to 50% in about 15 minutes. It’s also TÜV-certified, meaning an independent testing organization has verified its safety features.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger is up to 32% off from November 20 through December 1.

Sources indicate that for the student or anyone who does real work on an iPad, the ESR Shift Keyboard Case makes for an incredible gift. The Bluetooth keyboard attaches magnetically and comes off when you don’t need it, so you can type an essay at a desk, then pull the keyboard away to watch something on the couch or sketch with the iPad flat on a table.

According to recent reports, ESR built the Shift around five modes designed to make your iPad even more versatile. Productivity mode lets you detach the keyboard and type over Bluetooth, so the iPad can sit on a desk while the keyboard sits on your lap. Landscape mode adjusts from 20 to 75 degrees for typing and watching, Portrait mode holds 70 degrees for reading, browsing in Safari, or making a FaceTime call, and Drawing mode drops to a stable 20 degrees for sketching and editing with your Apple Pencil. Hands-On mode lets you hold the iPad like a regular tablet. An iPad is a laptop one minute and a tablet the next, and the Shift is designed to keep up with all of your iPad use cases.

For a student, that means taking notes in class with the keyboard attached, then detaching it to annotate a PDF or review flashcards on the couch. For someone who travels for work, it means answering email on a tray table, then pulling the keyboard off to watch a movie on the flight home. One case covers both, and the keyboard pairs and reconnects easily when you snap it back on.

It has been revealed that the trackpad is fully clickable and supports all the multi-touch gestures you already use on your iPad. Apple Pencil gets a home too. ESR’s Dual Smart Pencil Storage uses a magnetic holder and an elastic sleeve, so your Pencil stays with your iPad instead of rolling around the bottom of your bag. Its Air Guard corners protect your iPad when it’s stowed away.

The ESR Shift Keyboard Case comes in versions for iPad Pro 11-inch and 13-inch (M4 and M5), iPad Air 11-inch and 13-inch (including the newly introduced M4 models), and iPad (A16), so whichever iPad you’re trying to take to the next level of productivity, there’s a Shift that fits it.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Shift Keyboard Case is up to 25% off, depending on your iPad model.

It has been revealed that have you ever dropped your AirPods case and watched the earbuds go flying? With the Cyber FlickLock, you won’t have to worry about that. We’ve covered FlickLock in MagSafe Monday before, but let’s recap it.

Industry observers note that when the internal latch is engaged, the magnets line up to attract each other and hold the lid shut with maximum force, adding a second layer of security. Slide the button, and the magnets shift to repel each other, so the lid pops open with one hand. ESR claims the slide mechanism has been tested over 20,000 times.

According to recent reports, the result is that your AirPods stay in the case if you drop it. Both cases also have 260g of magnetic strength, so they snap onto MagSafe chargers, Apple Watch chargers, and MagSafe batteries if you need to charge your AirPods. Again, it’s extremely strong, but extremely easy to unlock with one hand.

The ESR Cyber FlickLock Magnetic Case is extremely durable and has a clip hook, so you can hang your AirPods on a backpack while hiking or cycling. The ESR Pulse FlickLock Magnetic Case brings the same lock in a range of vibrant colors with a carrying lanyard, so you can wear your AirPods on your wrist or attach them to a bag. Both cases come in versions for AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2 and 1, and AirPods 5 and 4. No matter which AirPods you or your loved one have, this is the case everyone will love.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Cyber FlickLock and Pulse FlickLock Magnetic Cases are both 20% off.

Recent findings suggest that the ESR Equinox Watch Band is a quick pick for anyone who works out in the morning while tracking progress with Apple Watch, then heads to the office. A pin-and-fold lock keeps it secure, and it’s made from HNBR, a durable, skin-friendly synthetic rubber that resists water and tearing, with ventilation cutouts for all-day comfort. It fits 44mm, 45mm, 46mm, and 49mm models across Apple Watch Ultra 1 through 4, Series 4 through 12, and SE 1 through 3, and it comes in several colors to match your outfit or your mood that day.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Equinox Watch Band is 20% off.

Sources indicate that the best gifts are the ones that get used every day, and accessories are the part of the Apple experience people live with the most. A case that props up a foldable, a screen protector made with Corning glass, a charger with a built-in cable, and an AirPods case that stays closed even when dropped check all the boxes. ESR truly makes something for everyone and is one of the most trusted names in the Apple accessories ecosystem.

Sources indicate that ESR built its Black Friday lineup around the whole Apple ecosystem, from the upcoming iPhone Duo to iPad, AirPods, and even a great Apple Watch band, with premium materials and versatile designs that are durable, functional, and great-looking. ESR’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals run on Amazon from November 19 through November 30 (the Xtend 45W runs through December 1), with discounts of up to 37%!

Be sure to follow ESR on X and Facebook to keep up with all of its latest products, deals, and more.

In a recent development, about Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Sources indicate that device management is built around the software IT deploys. Apps from Apple Business Manager, apps preloaded via your device management vendors’ packages, packages you upload, and profiles you push out. That model solves the problem for native macOS apps. It doesn’t cover what happens when the Mac becomes the default developer machine. Developers install what they need with a single command in Terminal, and Homebrew alone has more than 16,000 packages. You then add millions of npm packages and hundreds of thousands of IDE extensions, and the list of software on a Mac that IT didn’t put there is longer than the list it did.

That used to be a developer-only problem. It isn’t anymore, in the vibe-coding era. AI tools have turned marketers, analysts, and ops people into builders, and those builders install packages too.

Workbrew started as a management layer for Homebrew: an agent that reports what’s installed, flags known vulnerabilities, and lets IT push updates across the fleet. Version 2.0 expands the catalog to include npm packages, VS Code extensions, and macOS apps, all in a single inventory. The firm indicates it has patched more than 10 million vulnerabilities for customers since its launch, and it’s now ISO 27001-certified.

IT approves or denies in the Workbrew Console, and if it’s a no, the employee gets an answer on why.

The app comes from the Updatest team, which Workbrew acquired as part of this release. Updatest is the indie Mac app that keeps thousands of users’ software up to date, and it remains a separate product for individuals and families. For business customer, that experience is now the Workbrew app, and it’s included on every plan, including the free Team plan with no device or user limits.

In a recent development, with Workbrew, we finally have real visibility into what developers are using in Homebrew. Fleet-wide updates are effortless, and the team stays secure without being slowed down.

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo have been out for quite some time now, and despite that, it’s still incredibly challenging to order an iPhone Duo in a timely manner. If for whatever reason you’re considering skipping out on this year’s iPhones, here’s what you have to look forward to next year.

According to recent reports, 2027 is going to be a relatively major iPhone release year for Apple. First, the tech giant will be continuing the iPhone 18 lineup after it introduced a split release schedule. Then, in the fall, the company will debut a latest round of flagships in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. Here’s what to expect.

For the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring. Upgrades for the iPhone 18 aren’t quite clear, though more RAM is one of the key rumors. Thermal upgrades will likely happen as well, as well as the new Apple C2 modem.

It’s possible Apple will enhancement the design to fall more in line with the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro, though we don’t yet know.

This phone will of course equip the A20 chip, and it’ll probably start at the same $899 price point that iPhone 17 presently sits at – after it was increased from $799 in September.

Recent findings suggest that this phone will most likely just end up being a chip bump from the A19 to A20 chip, and debut in the Spring alongside the iPhone 18. Earlier this year, reports indicated that Apple would share many components between the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, though it isn’t quite clear what that could mean for the devices.

Out of all of the spring iPhone releases, this one is the one to look forward to. After receiving a lukewarm reception with the initial iPhone Air model, Apple went back to the drawing board and decided to modify the design to fit an ultrawide camera into the device.

Recent findings suggest that personally, I don’t think an ultrawide camera is too important – though many people will see one camera on the back of the phone and immediately assume it’s less premium, so it’ll probably end up being an important upgrade for the sake of sales. Plus, ultrawide photos can be fun at times.

In a recent development, it should also have a larger battery, reportedly as large as 3500mAh. That’s a roughly 10% improvement from the original iPhone Air. iPhone Air 2 will likely also jump from Apples C1X modem to the C2.

For the 20th anniversary of the iPhone, Apple is expected to debut a fully redesigned iPhone to celebrate. It’ll reportedly be much more glassy, feature significantly slimmer bezels, a quad curved display, and ditch the flat edge design of the iPhone 12 and later.

Industry observers note that personally, I’m slightly skeptical that this’ll truly be a replacement to the “Pro” phone for thermal reasons, but time will tell. iPhone Duo seemingly has strong thermals while not featuring an aluminum unibody, so my concern might not be relevant. It’ll offer two, larger display sizes: 6.4-inch and 7-inch. This largely comes from the bezel reduction.

Recent findings suggest that I wish they prioritized the Telephoto camera more. I need that (whether it be on an Air or a Duo) way more than an Ultrawide.

If you’re holding out for iPhone 18 Pro, this “iPhone 20” is definitely the phone to wait out for.

Lastly, Apple will release a successor to its just-announced iPhone Duo next fall. Of course, you can expect next-generation Apple Silicon with the A21 Pro chip next year, but there aren’t many other substantial changes expected. Apple may bring proper Face ID to the outer display, an improvement from the recently-announced face unlock, but it’s unclear whether this feature will make the engineering cutoff date.

Cento fine foods has been sued for “tomato fraud”

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slate

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • So you’ve decided to make homemade pasta sauce.
  • Industry observers note that first stop: browsing the supermarket for the best canned tomatoes for your future marinara.
  • You’ve heard that phrase before somewhere—the Food Network?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So you’ve decided to make homemade pasta sauce. Good for you, chef!

Industry observers note that first stop: browsing the supermarket for the best canned tomatoes for your future marinara. Now you’re deciding between Hunt’s, Mutti, Bianco DiNapoli, Cento, DeLallo, and those nondescript cans of tomatoes from The Bear filled with wads of cash. You’re considering brands, price points, and whether to buy your tomatoes whole-peeled, crushed, or diced, or hmm … maybe that jar of Rao’s would be easier? Then, just when you’re about to give up, two little words on a label stand out: San Marzano.

You’ve heard that phrase before somewhere—the Food Network? Ina Garten? That’s supposed to be primo stuff, right? Probably can’t go wrong with tomatoes that are actually from Italy. They’re a few dollars more expensive than the domestic options, but you spring for a can or two anyway. Surely getting the real thing will be worth the hassle and cost once that first forkful of al dente pasta and perfect sauce hits your lips.

Sources indicate that san Marzano tomatoes are indeed considered the good shit. They’re cherished for their low water content (think naturally saucy, thick tomatoes), their sweetness, and their deeply savory flavor—all qualities that can make or break a marinara. And they are certainly Italian: San Marzano tomatoes come from the Agro Sarnese-Nocerino region of southwest Italy, home to the fertile land surrounding Mount Vesuvius, the volcano that once destroyed Pompeii but whose ashy eruptions, settling over time into a nutrient-dense soil, now more helpfully produce the prized fruits in question.

According to recent reports, authentic San Marzano tomatoes are regulated—at least in Europe—by the Consorzio di Tutela del Pomodoro San Marzano dell’Agro Sarnese-Nocerino DOP, which I will be shortening to “the Consortium” so we don’t all go insane. And the Consortium is serious about its job. According to its regulations, true San Marzanos must have an elongated shape that usually measures between 6 and 8 centimeters and demonstrate that classic balance of sweet and tart flavor. The thin skin peels off easily, enclosing dense, fleshy pulp with very few seeds. They must possess something called an axis ratio of no less than 2.2 + 0.2, or contain limited presence of “placental voids,” which means the seed cavities are filled with gelatinous tomato gel and pulp rather than empty space. In short, they’re the jackpot if you are looking to make an unforgettably robust sauce or lip-smacking soup, and the Consortium exists solely to be this marvelous tomato’s protector.

There’s a reason these elite tomatoes are so tightly controlled. They can be grown only in a tiny region of the world—fewer than 1,000 acres of eligible volcano-adjacent land are presently cultivated—so they’re in very short supply. Or at least they ought to be. A skeptic might ask how the hell such prestigious produce ended up available in bulk at your local Ralphs or Whole Foods. Are all the brands touting the name actually San Marzanos? Is that even possible?

Recent findings suggest that according to a recent lawsuit, the answer is … not necessarily. In fact, some of them are almost certainly fake. It’s been called “tomato fraud,” and it’s a real problem in the U.S. Fraud may seem like a dramatic word to apply to a tin of tomatoes, but given the considerably higher cost of cans labeled “San Marzano” (recently between $6 and $8, compared to between $3 and $5 for a normie 28-oz. can in my local market), where there are fakes, honest consumers are being ripped off by companies looking to profit from a legendary culinary reputation that isn’t theirs to claim. And tomato snobs aren’t taking it lying down.

Recent findings suggest that over the past 10 years or so, lawsuits accusing brands of tomato deceit have become quite ordinary. Take, for example, the highly entertaining San Merican lawsuit. The short version is that a manufacturer named Simpson Brands in Pennsylvania labeled its cans “SMT,” and in exquisitely sneaky fine print, the text by each letter spelled “San Merican Tomatoes,” instead of “San Marzano.” Though the plaintiff ultimately dropped the suit (and Simpson denied the allegations), I think its claim—that a reasonable person could easily confuse these impostors with the genuine article—is certainly fair. (Oh, and by the way, those San Merican tomatoes are trash. Not even close to San Marzanos. San Mericans are watery and sour Roma tomatoes, not the thick, sweet San Marzano variety. How to tell? Squeeze one of the San Mericans in your hand, and it’ll burst everywhere as if you just unloaded a shotgun on a jar of Prego.).

Sources indicate that while you do see “San Marzano–style” tomatoes sold quite frequently, as this verbiage merely refers to the botanical genus of the tomato and passes muster in the U.S. (somewhat like the general cheese term “Parmesan” vs. Parmigiano-Reggiano, which has its own official minders), straight-up labeling something San Marzano that isn’t would seem to run afoul of false-advertising prohibitions and leave violators open to litigation. (The Consortium might not like it, but it has no power this side of the Atlantic.) So you’d think companies would, you know, avoid doing that. Just stand behind the tomatoes you’ve got.

But there’s one well-known brand that may have thrown caution to the wind. It’s one you’ve definitely seen on your grocery store shelves, one that’s available in both old-school Italian delis and high-end grocers alike. And it may have succeeded in duping everybody—at least according to the folks suing it for $25 million in damages. In the eyes of these litigants, the dignity of the Rolls-Royce of tomatoes—and the integrity of America’s food system—is on the line. The questions they raise about product quality, corporate transparency, and the weight of authenticity could shape what we stir into our pots and spoon into our mouths for years to come.

In early May, a lawsuit was filed against Cento Fine Foods Inc., claiming that the firm’s iconic yellow cans of tomatoes sold as San Marzano can’t possibly be the real deal: Cento Fine Foods, a Newly introduced Jersey–based company, versus Natalie Gianne of Los Angeles and Mike Aldrich of Whittier, California. The crux of the suit is that authentic San Marzano tomatoes possess physical characteristics that render them superior to other tomatoes, and so what’s in Cento’s cans is simply not that. The filing alleges that Cento’s tomatoes “lack the taste, consistency, and other physical characteristics associated by consumers with certified San Marzano Tomatoes.” Thus, they were deemed “unsatisfactory” to the plaintiffs, who never would have paid a premium for them had they known the truth. And naturally (this is America), they’re seeking millions of dollars in flavor harm.

It has been revealed that in a statement to Slate, Cento said that it “refutes all of the inaccurate and wrongful claims” in the complaint, calling it “entirely without merit.” The organization added that it is seeking a “prompt dismissal” of the suit. The Weston Firm, the lawyers representing the plaintiffs, did not respond to requests for an interview.

It has been revealed that if this all sounds kind of hard to prove in court, I’d say you’re right—taste is subjective. But that’s where the Consortium is supposed to come in. In 1996, the European Union granted the Consortium the exclusive right to certify and approve San Marzano tomatoes, empowering it to stamp authentic cans with a DOP/PDO label (meaning Product of Designated Origin). When you see that seal, you are being promised that what’s inside is verified. And Italians live to protect their products. They protect their cheese with DOP labeling, and they even have their own pizza rules: See the AVPN (the True Neapolitan Pizza Association), which aims to tell you what a Neapolitan pizza is and, more importantly, what it isn’t. In this case, the AVPN, which approves true Neapolitan pizzerias through a rigorous application process, even goes so far as to dispatch secret agents to later spy on pizzerias. If they aren’t meeting the organization’s high standards, they’re delisted. The Consortium, meanwhile, also inspects, approves, and occasionally delists tomato purveyors with the same critical eye.

So Italy has made rules for its San Marzano tomatoes, and Europe enforces them, at least in theory. Over there, you can’t just 3D-print some tomatoes, put them in a can, and call them San Marzanos. If you did, you would be the subject of police or judicial raids (which, as we’ll see, Cento may know something about). Here in the U.S., however, those rules don’t apply: There is technically no legal protection of that term as such, which is why alleging false advertising or consumer fraud—not getting the product you think you’re paying for—would be a shopper’s only avenue for justice against perceived trickery. This Gianne-Aldrich lawsuit argues that the Consortium is the only entity that can certify and approve San Marzano tomatoes grown in Italy, and here’s the thing: Cento is not acknowledged as a legitimate producer by the Consortium. Meanwhile, the firm doesn’t even hedge and label its tomatoes San Marzano–style. Cento seems to be saying, “Bitch, these are San Marzanos,” and then raising its fist in the hope you’ll flinch.

Industry observers note that how does Cento do it? Well, according to the lawsuit, it goes around the Consortium completely and has a third party certify its tomatoes (a process that, for its part, the company defends in detail on a dedicated webpage—one that clarifies, in very small print, that its certification partner is not affiliated with any consortium). That’s why its cans read “Certified” but don’t feature the official DOP seal. Feels shady, no? Why did Cento sidestep the Consortium to begin with? If its product is authentic, why not just obtain that official seal to avoid such headaches?

The answer is where things get real juicy: Cento used to be a participant in the Consortium, but over a decade ago it was reportedly ejected from the organization for what certainly looks like—you guessed it—tomato fraud.

In 2010, according to the current lawsuit, “police in Salerno obtained a criminal search warrant and raided Cento’s Italian operations.” What they found were 144,000 cans of intentionally mislabeled tomatoes. Manager Giuseppe Napoletano was busted for distributing tomatoes bearing counterfeit DOP labeling. Napoletano was also found to have “forged the signatures of tomato farmers” and to have “repeatedly committed fraud in order to obtain false certifications.” In 2019, an Italian court found Napoletano and his father, an accomplice, guilty of criminal fraud, for which they received fines and were given 26-month suspended sentences. What’s not clear is whether Napoletano did these things at Cento’s direction or acted alone. In my research, I found no evidence that Cento has ever commented on the incident directly, though it has characterized its exit from the Consortium as voluntary. Moreover, when I emailed the firm to get a comment on Napoletano and the fraud, I heard nothing back.

Industry observers note that but San Marzano tomatoes are a moneymaker, a prestige purchase for foodies everywhere. Cento clearly couldn’t lose its cash cow. After exiting the Consortium, though, claiming that it was hawking authentic San Marzanos would be tricky. The solution, according to the lawsuit: Get its tomatoes blessed by a “third-party certifier” called “Agri-Cert.”.

“The hell is Agri-Cert?” I asked while reading the official court documents. Soon, I found myself obsessing over the organization’s comings and goings, its staff, its operations. Near as I can tell, the organization (also known, and findable online, as Bioagricert, which I’ll use going forward) seems to have one gig, and that gig is certification. It stamps products as organic, vegan, regenerative, and the like. But it also certifies traceability, meaning it traces an ingredient to its source. The lawsuit against Cento claims that Bioagricert doesn’t “possess the capabilities” to ensure that Cento’s products meet the same specifications as those overseen by the Consortium. Nonetheless, the plaintiffs have submitted photographic evidence of labels and website copy from Cento that call out Bioagricert (styled “Agri-Cert”) as its third-party certifier by name.

Recent findings suggest that so what’s the deal with this mysterious outfit? After weeks of attempting to make contact, I finally got a response from the organization that may have sliced this can wide open. Technical manager Salvatore Sergi explained its relationship to Cento via email, which … well, read it for yourself.

“We do not certify Cento products,” Sergi wrote. “Rather, we certify an Italian firm exclusively for the ISO 22005 standard (supply chain traceability). The peeled tomatoes are sold in the United States by our certified company inside unlabeled cans. These products are accompanied by a certificate that makes no reference to San Marzano tomatoes, as they are protected by PDO status throughout Europe. Cento applies its own label to the anonymous cans directly in the U.S. (where there is no protection for PDOs), due to the lack of a mutual recognition agreement with the EU.”.

He summed it up in one sentence: “In conclusion, our certification is valid only in Italy for our tech giant.”.

According to recent reports, to recap, Bioagricert certifies the traceability of the tomatoes—where they come from, yes (which might be crucial in, say, an outbreak of foodborne illness), and in this case, Cento’s assertion that they are grown in the correct region. Bioagricert does not, as Cento arguably insinuates with its labeling, certify that these are true San Marzanos with the same detailed Consortium characteristics (though Cento does claim to adhere to some of them, such as length, independently). And it doesn’t certify that because it literally can’t. That’s the Consortium’s territory. What’s more, Sergi states, the cans arrive in the U.S. unlabeled. It is only in America that Cento apparently applies the “San Marzano” and “Certified” labels. (Cento’s site claims the tech giant has a “production facility” in “Campania’s San Marzano growing region.”).

In any case, you, chef, should not have to be concerned with tracing the international supply chain. You are in the pasta aisle. You pick up one of those yellow cans. There’s no DOP/PDO label; instead, there’s a green ribbon with the word Certified struck across it. Confusing? Yes, but as with a lot of products sold in America—from honey to olive oil—our government states you, the consumer, are required to read the fine print. Again, this shouldn’t be an matter: An entire organization exists to protect San Marzano tomatoes. Alas, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration doesn’t play by Europe’s rules, and vice versa—according to an investigation by the Italian news station RAI 3, Cento’s “San Marzano” tomatoes wouldn’t actually be able to be sold in Italy. It would be illegal to label them as such.

In a recent development, back across the Atlantic, will Cento finally pay the piper? Andrich et al. v. Cento Fine Foods Inc. is still undecided, but I should note that a much more scathing lawsuit from 2019 was thrown out. That one claims that the “Find My Field” tracker on the back of each Cento can—which you can use, CIA-style, to locate the exact coordinates your tomato came from—takes you to the same four fields over and over again. “It is implausible that [the] defendant can sell more San Marzano tomatoes than all other companies in the U.S., combined, and do so by cultivating only four fields,” the suit read.

Industry observers note that implausible indeed, but a New York judge dismissed the case, citing that your average person wouldn’t expect San Marzanos to be labeled with the Consortium’s DOP seal: “Here, while there may be ‘some few consumers’ who expect that a San Marzano tomato must be certified by the Consortium, the Court concludes, drawing upon common sense and common experience, that the vast majority of reasonable consumers expect no such thing. It is much more likely that consumers expect tomatoes grown in a region of Italy.”.

Perhaps. But one rule I live by is that you should never assume that your audience is dumb. While your average person might be unaware of tomato fraud, people who care about food care about what they’re buying. And with each passing lawsuit and news story, it’s getting harder to buy that we’re getting true San Marzanos at all. In fact, the whole thing has me second-guessing my entire tomato reality.

At this point, you might want me to answer: Which brands of San Marzanos are trustworthy? We could consult the Consortium, of course, but I’m starting to think that may not be the right question. That, instead, might be: At the end of the day, when you’re just trying to get dinner on the table in your own kitchen, does any of this alleged tomato fraud even matter? Who, if anybody, is hurt by it?

It has been revealed that well, for starters, I would say that the farmers in the Agro Sarnese-Nocerino are deeply affected. These are generations of San Marzano growers. Many of the farmers are handpicking the tomatoes without using machines. A San Marzano tomato isn’t only its genus; its identity is fully wrapped up in the process of growing and harvesting—the region, the soil, and the methods of the farming itself. So long as San Marzano imitators exist, then the work of these hardworking farmers will be undervalued. In addition, Italian brands like Gustarosso, Casa Marrazzo, and Flora, which all adhere to the Consortium’s rules, are undercut by fakes.

But personally speaking, I find myself with a moral dilemma. Because, friends, in my opinion as a food writer and avid pasta-maker, I have to confess: Cento’s “San Marzano” tomatoes are actually excellent. They are, near as I can tell, the best available tomato at the most supermarket chains. I’ve praised Cento in similar terms in the past, before undertaking this head-spinning journey into the gelatinous placental void, but even knowing what I know now, the fact remains that Cento’s tomatoes are sweet, savory, deep, and saucy. They are perfect for a red sauce. And I’m not the only one who thinks so.

“Before I opened SheWolf, I tried over 50 cans of tomatoes,” indicates Anthony Lombardo, chef and owner of acclaimed Italian restaurants Medusa and Shewolf in Detroit, “and Cento was the best.” That’s high praise not only because of Lombardo’s expert taste as a professional, but also because he has gone further than most in trying to capture that San Marzano essence here at home.

“It’s not like cheese or wine or salami,” he claims, “where the DOP or DOC has real validity because it has to be this grape, has to come from this species of animal, or be this exact milk to be called this cheese.” Lombardo’s point is that tomato seeds are easily grown in other climates. Hell, I just saw a sign for “San Marzano tomatoes” at the Santa Monica farmers market, and a woman walking past exclaimed to her partner, “Oooh! San Marzanos!”.

Industry observers note that lombardo may or may not have recently smuggled some San Marzano seeds back directly from Italy, which he may or may not grow at an urban farm in Core City, a few miles outside Detroit’s downtown area. He indicates me a picture of green plum tomatoes growing on a vine, which he has dubbed “Detroit San Marzanos.” “Literally the opposite of a volcano,” he says of their terroir. I ask Lombardo, who has ventured to Italy numerous times, if his Detroit varietal tastes the same as true, Consortium-certified San Marzanos. “They do not,” he says. So will the tomato police come for Lombardo? Probably not, because of the 80-some tomato plants he has, which are thriving, none of the fruit will be labeled and served as San Marzano tomatoes. Smart man.

“I get why [the Consortium] are pissed. This is, like, their thing,” he admits. “But what do I call this tomato that is clearly the shape and size of a San Marzano?” It’s a great question. San Marzano–style? Sans Marzanos? Marzano di Detroit? Is the distinction even key when we live in a country where so many things are mislabeled?

Italians argue that it’s not just their genealogy that makes their prize fruits San Marzanos, but their terroir. Their land. It’s that sweet, sweet volcanic soil, and the lore that comes with it, that everyone is so horny for. But more than that, it’s the culture of Italy that is worthy of being protected. Their very identity is wrapped up in these tomatoes, and when nefarious operations find a loophole, well, it can feel as if they’re crushing that identity in the palms of their hands like an Italian nonna making red sauce.

I get all that. And yet … I’ll say it again: Cento is right now selling the best can of tomatoes—widely available, anyway—here in the U.S. While arguably not up to Italy’s standards, the tomatoes are still wonderful in flavor and texture. These are fleshy, elongated fruits dunked in a viscous sauce, with a deeply savory flavor one would expect of, gulp, San Marzanos. I pick one up, squeeze it softly and let the plum tomato break apart gently in my palm. It doesn’t burst with water. It just sort of dissolves. I eat a piece right from the can. It’s thick and sweet, and perhaps that judge was right: It’s so good that I can’t find it in me to care about where exactly it comes from. And ultimately, I feel a little ashamed about that.

But should I? I understand the value of cultural heritage, and in my heart of hearts, I wish we lived in a world that cared about authenticity, or even just the concept of a shared reality. But I don’t have to tell you that’s not where we are. Do I hope Gianne and Aldrich win their lawsuit? If their claims of fraud are true, then, yes, justice should be served. I’m tired, nay, exhausted, of living in a country where we’re constantly questioning what’s real. Where the people in charge have us second-guessing our good sense. I will concede that if this all comes down to a simple taste test, then Cento’s tomatoes are quite good. But I’d be fully willing to trade that quality for some goddamn clarity. For some honesty. For something tangible and trustworthy that I can pick up and hold. Without that, it’s hard to enjoy how good the food may taste.

Recent findings suggest that so, I will simply ask Cento one thing: If the produce in the yellow cans are not bona fide San Marzanos, just drop the ruse, man. Drop the wishy-washy “Certified” label, and let the tomatoes do the talking—they can definitely speak for themselves! That way, we can all shut up, stop clogging up the courts, and get back to the thing we want to do most: making some damn pasta.

Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on one port

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Frankchiarulli

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I started building restorekit.org dongles a few months ago at the Recurse Center.
  • The original board, the Dongle-Lite, is USB 2 only.
  • Sources indicate that I recently learned from timo at Twocanoes that newer Macs support USB 3 speeds for recovery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I started building restorekit.org dongles a few months ago at the Recurse Center. They are small inline USB-C boards that sit between a host computer and a target mac. They set the target mac into DFUDevice Firmware Update: Apple's lowest-level recovery mode built into the boot ROM, so even a bricked Mac can be reflashed. mode over USB-PDUSB Power Delivery: the communication protocol over the CC wire used to negotiate power, roles, and vendor-defined commands. without having to touch the target at all, and work with an open-source toolkit for restoring macs without the need for another mac.

The original board, the Dongle-Lite, is USB 2 only. A single USB 2 hub (CH334F) connects both the dongle’s MCU and the target mac through a single cable, while a PD PHYPhysical-layer transceiver chip that encodes and decodes USB Power Delivery packets on the CC wire. (FUSB302B) sends Apple’s DFU commands on the CC line.

Sources indicate that I recently learned from timo at Twocanoes that newer Macs support USB 3 speeds for recovery. I obviously immediately wanted to support this on the hub for faster recovery, but the problem was cost. At first I designed a “proper” USB 3 board using a GL3510 USB 3 hub and a pair of TI SuperSpeed muxes (HD3SS3220 and HD3SS3212). It basically doubled the parts count, and BOMBill of Materials: the full list of components and quantities required to assemble one board. cost, required me to increase the size of PCB to ~100 mm, and topped out at 5 Gbps transfers between host and target (USB 3.1 Gen 1).

I really didn’t want to make a board that cost more than twice the Dongle-Lite just to get USB 3 speeds.

So with the 2nd version Dongle-Pro, I tried a kinda crazy USB-C experiment: drop the USB 3 hub completely, keep a cheap USB 2 hub on D+/D-, and route the USB 3 SuperSpeedUSB 3.x's dedicated high-speed TX/RX differential pairs, physically separate from USB 2's D+/D- wires. lanes as a straight passthrough from host to target on the same USB-C port. The idea being that in theory the USB 3 and 2 controllers on a USB-C are completely independent, and should work simultaneously.

Since high-speed USB 3 is super prone to interference I didn’t really have a choice other than to purchase a view boards and test it out.

Well… I just got the boards in from JLC and… THEY WORK! They establish a full 10 Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 connection while connecting the dongle’s USB 2 hub and MCU over the exact same port. After some aggressive cost optimization, the 10 Gbps board also ended up cheaper and smaller than the USB 2 Dongle-Lite.

In a recent development, like I mentioned earlier, USB-C is not a single data bus. Inside a standard USB-C port, USB 2 and USB 3 sit on completely different sets of pins:.

Every USB-C port has two mirrored 12-pin rows: A1 through A12 on top, and B12 through B1 on the bottom, so a cable works rotated either way.

This continues to the computer’s xHCIExtensible Host Controller Interface: the USB controller inside your computer that manages both USB 2 and USB 3.x root ports. controller: a single physical USB-C port is actually wired to two independent root ports: a USB 2 port and a USB 3 port.

Industry observers note that A standard USB 3 hub chip like the GL3510 is actually just two hubs in 1 package (a USB 2 hub and a USB 3 hub). On my first iteration of the Dongle-Pro, everything ran through that chip even though the dongle’s own MCU only speaks USB 2 Full Speed (12 Mbps) and has no need for the USB 3 speed.

On the Dongle-Pro v2, the two buses are split apart:.

This sounded like it would work to me on paper, but there were a few things I thought could go wrong:.

When the boards arrived, I immediately plugged one into my mac, plugged an iPhone into the target port, and inspected the bus with system_profiler SPUSBHostDataType and ioreg -p IOUSB.

Here is what macOS sees on a single physical USB-C port (AppleT8132USBXHCI@01000000):.

The raw system_profiler SPUSBHostDataType output shows both sides active at once:.

Industry observers note that 0x01100000 is the USB 2 half of the physical port, and 0x01200000 is the SuperSpeed half of the same port. The iPhone enumerated straight through both passive CH9441P muxes at 10 Gb/s (USB 3.2 Gen 2), while the CH334P hub and Dongle-Pro-v2 MCU enumerate at 480 Mb/s and 12 Mb/s on D+/D-.

Splitting the bus required one interesting change in the host SDK (restorekit).

Industry observers note that on the Dongle-Lite, whatever device you plugged into the dongle always showed up as a child of the dongle’s hub. That made it easy to tell which target Mac belonged to which dongle when you plugged in several at once.

It has been revealed that on the Dongle-Pro v2, that breaks whenever the target connects at USB 3. Just like iPhone@01200000 above, a SuperSpeed target bypasses the CH334P hub completely and demonstrates up as a sibling directly on the host’s root hub.

Turns out the OS already tracks which USB 2 and USB 3 root ports share the same physical port and it exposes it directly:.

So restorekit can still know with 100% certainty which 10 Gbps device is plugged into which dongle.

I originally planned to have a Dongle-Lite and significantly more expensive USB 3 Pro, but that means having to maintain two hardware lines, so if I could cut the cost of the USB 3 version to be comparably priced to the original Dongle-Lite it felt like a no brainer.

After I removed the GL3510 USB 3 hub from the original design, I went through the rest of the board to see what else I could cut:.

Running the three BOMs against JLCPCB pricing:.

(Parts and Extended feeder fees from JLCPCB’s catalog, excluding PCB fab and placement fees. V2 wins on fab cost too since it is 40% smaller than the Lite and 60% smaller than Pro v1, packing three boards into one 81 x 48 mm panel.).

These swaps resulted in a 72% BOM reduction from original Dongle-Pro while doubling the SuperSpeed link rate from 5 Gbps to 10 Gbps, and a 42% BOM reduction compared to the Dongle-Lite.

In a recent development, if you are building an inline USB-C tool where your MCU only needs a slow control channel and the host just needs fast passthrough to the downstream device, you might not need a USB 3 hub. USB-C gives you two independent buses in the same port.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Flipper One crowdfunding campaign has broken the $13-million mark, smashing the funding raised for previous Flipper devices and demonstrating strong interest in the successor to the Flipper Zero. The $399 Flipper One is a pocket Linux computer focused on networking, with delivery estimated for July 2027. But it isn’t simply an updated version of the Flipper Zero. It’s a very different animal and a much more serious bit of kit.

The thing that made the Flipper Zero so popular was how easy it was to use. You could fire it up and turn the volume down on the TV at your parents’ place, see the radio waves coming from your car’s key fob, and copy hotel room key cards.

Also: The Flipper One may be the ultimate Linux PC for hackers in 2026 – and I’m excited.

Industry observers note that it could do a lot, there wasn’t a steep learning curve, and you didn’t need to buy anything else. Did the fake videos on TikTok from people claiming they could change the prices at gas stations (I wish!) or start cars remotely help make the Zero more popular?

According to recent reports, unfortunately, yes. But what made it successful was that it packed a lot of power into a package that was small, fun, affordable, and easy to use.

If the Flipper Zero, with its NFC, RFID, sub-GHz, and IR, was kindergarten, the Flipper One is a college degree: a pocket Linux computer focused on networking.

This is reflected in the price. You can pick up a Zero for $169, while the Flipper One is $399.

What this buys you is the Flipper One base computer with a 256 × 144 grayscale LCD, Rockchip RK3576 8-core ARM SoC with NPU, a low-power MCU for handling the LCD and user interface, 8GB of LPDDR5 RAM, 64GB of UFS 2.2 storage, and a microSD slot.

If that $399 feels like a lot, it’s worth keeping in mind that, according to Flipper, the price only covers production costs and that the RAM and UFS storage account for at least half of the total hardware cost.

Industry observers note that if you think this is a lot, you could spend a lot more. Adding a LoRa, SDR, or 5G module will push the total up a lot higher. And if you want all three modules, you’re looking at $759 for the Flipper One Ultimate Bundle.

Also: The Flipper One is the Linux cyberdeck I wish my Raspberry Pi could be.

Industry observers note that the reception has been strong enough that pledges have flown past the $300,000 goal that Flipper initially set, with over 24,000 backers pledging over $13 million. Close to 5,300 backers have gone for the Ultimate Bundle, compared to just over 4,300 choosing the bare Flipper One.

This suggests that backers really want the radio capabilities that this upcoming platform offers.

If you want one, this crowdfunding run is a good time to get one because it’s a Kickstarter Special slashing 25% off an estimated retail price of $550.

The response over on Reddit has been a little more subdued, with some being taken aback by the price of the Zero’s bigger sibling.

Also: 7 useful things I can do with my Flipper Zero – as someone who’s used it for years.

As someone who homebrews a lot of electronics, I’m going to say that the price is justified, and this project goes far beyond something you could put together with a Raspberry Pi and some code.

It has been revealed that the Flipper One campaign runs until Dec. 17, 2026, with delivery estimated for July 2027.

In a recent development, keep in mind that this is a Kickstarter pledge, not a purchase, and that rewards aren’t guaranteed. Flipper also claims on the Kickstarter page that component shortages are the biggest risk to the project and that they “could cause significant delays to production and delivery.” It also says that if RAM prices continue to rise, it cannot “rule out adjusting some product specifications, including reducing the amount of RAM.”.

Also: Is the Flipper Zero the best multi-tool for hacking?

And the good news here is that I’ve seen several analysts predicting that RAM prices will begin to go down in 2027 as demand eases off.

Recent findings suggest that the popular animation featuring realistic aquarium life will be replaced by the Roku City screensaver on Dec. 1. Roku City is the platform’s signature purple skyline, featuring rotating digital billboards packed with brand sponsorships and clever pop-culture Easter eggs. (Seattle’s short-spined raccoon, Jimothy, has made an appearance.).

According to recent reports, that doesn’t mean all fish-filled options have been flushed. Several third-party Roku wallpaper apps offer a variety of aquarium options to choose from. But if you’re sticking to what Roku itself provides on its streaming boxes, the move away from the aquarium screensaver also means switching to an alternative that’s filled with advertising.

“It seems like this is a way for Roku to convert a popular screensaver into a way to make money, or at least generate more engagement, via the Roku City version,” said CNET Senior Editor Ty Pendlebury, who covers home entertainment options including the Roku streaming boxes.

A Roku representative didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Viewers who miss these specific fish can still watch a YouTube version of Roku’s Aquatic Life screensaver for as long as the organization chooses to keep this nearly 3-minute video on the internet.

The Aquatic Life screensaver loss is a drop in the ocean compared to other changes at the streamer this year. Roku was purchased by Fox for $22 billion in June, which puts the streaming platform under the same ownership as Fox’s Tubi and Fox One channels. That deal is expected to close in 2027.

Hierarchical Bayesian Neural Networks: When Structure Meets Flexibility

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (435 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Statwonk

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a previous post, we showed that Bayesian hierarchical models (BHMs) win when group structure is describable, Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) win when the signal is complex, and their ensemble hedges across both scenarios.
  • But what about the case where your data has both — known group structure and complex nonlinear signal?
  • Industry observers note that enter the hierarchical Bayesian neural network (HBNN) — a model that combines partial pooling over groups with a flexible neural network function class.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a previous post, we showed that Bayesian hierarchical models (BHMs) win when group structure is describable, Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) win when the signal is complex, and their ensemble hedges across both scenarios.

But what about the case where your data has both — known group structure and complex nonlinear signal? Neither the BHM nor the BNN is ideal:.

Industry observers note that enter the hierarchical Bayesian neural network (HBNN) — a model that combines partial pooling over groups with a flexible neural network function class. This post adds the HBNN to our comparison and shows when each of the four approaches excels.

The HBNN adds partially-pooled group intercepts to the neural network. The non-centered parameterization lets Stan explore the posterior efficiently:.

Line by line, this is a BNN with one addition: alpha[g[n]] — a group-specific intercept drawn from a learned population distribution. The neural network learns the shared nonlinear signal f(x), and the hierarchical intercepts capture group-level shifts. Each component does what it's best at.

The signal is linear and the heterogeneity is in group-specific intercepts and slopes. The BHM is perfectly specified — its functional form matches the DGP exactly. The HBNN's neural network component adds unnecessary flexibility here, making it a close second but slightly less efficient due to the additional parameters.

Recent findings suggest that no group-level heterogeneity — the group labels are noise. Both the BHM and the HBNN waste capacity estimating group intercepts that don't exist, but the BNN focuses entirely on learning the nonlinear signal. The HBNN is close because partial pooling drives the unnecessary group intercepts toward zero, but the BNN's simpler parameterization gives it an edge.

Now the data has both group-specific offsets and a complex nonlinear signal. This is the scenario the HBNN was built for:.

↓ Lower CRPS = lower out-of-sample prediction error (winner).

The HBNN isn't always the best model — it's the best model when the data has the structure it's designed for. That's the No Free Lunch theorem in action: every model has a niche, and the art is matching the model to the problem.

In a recent development, in domains like portfolio optimization, clinical trials, and marketing mix modeling, the data often has exactly this structure: known grouping variables (sectors, treatment arms, channels) with complex nonlinear effects. The HBNN architecture — encoding the structure you know and learning the rest — represents a principled middle ground between pure specification and pure flexibility.

According to recent reports, the complete R script is available at hbnn_comparison_reprex.R. It requires cmdstanr, scoringRules, and tidyverse. Runtime is approximately 4–5 minutes.

Energy Transfer (ET) is a diversified midstream energy company with about 140,000 miles of pipelines and associated energy infrastructure in 44 states. The company made a quarterly cash distribution of 34 cents per common unit for the second quarter of 2026. At an annualized payment of $1.36 per common unit, ET offers a yield of 6.3%.

Recently, JPMorgan analyst Jeremy Tonet reiterated a buy rating on Energy Transfer stock and slightly raised his price target to $25 from $24. The analyst noted that the tech giant delivered a strong Q2 beat across all key metrics.

Tonet highlighted that Energy Transfer raised its 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to $18.8 billion-$19.1 billion from $18.2 billion-$18.6 billion, reflecting robust base results and cost optimization. The 5-star analyst added that the company "tightened" its capex to $5.6 billion–$5.9 billion and expects capex above $5 billion annually through 2029, given solid opportunities.

About the Hugh Brinson pipeline, Tonet noted Phase 1 (1.5 bcfd) reaching full capacity by September 1 and Phase II capacity (0.7 bcfd) going online by Q1 2027. The analyst also noted completion of a 14-mile Hugh Brinson lateral in Abilene, Texas, and final stages of talks for an additional 250 mmcfd of Oklahoma power plant demand.

"All in, we see ET well positioned to continue capitalizing on organic growth opportunities across the value chain," noted Tonet.

Tonet ranks No. 922 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 9%. See Energy Transfer Financials on TipRanks.

This week's second dividend pick is independent oil and natural gas company Permian Resources (PR). The company declared a base dividend of $0.16 per share for the third quarter, payable on September 30, 2026. At an annualized dividend of $0.64 per share, PR offers a yield of about 2.7%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Permian Resources stock and increased his price target to $27 from $22, citing an improved outlook on oil production growth and operational efficiencies.

Sources indicate that the 5-star analyst noted that while PR stock has outperformed its peers so far in 2026, he sees further upside. Mehta is confident about the firm's operational improvements and ability to deliver incremental free cash flow per share through the strategic ground game program. He added that the program has completed about $1.05 billion in bolt-on deals this year (as of August 5).

"We see the continued success of PR's ground game as constructive toward future inventory replenishment and increasing working interest over time," remarked Mehta.

The analyst also emphasized Permian Resources' solid track record of generating growth in free cash flow (FCF) per share. Mehta expects the company's free cash flow per share to grow at a 20% CAGR (compound annual growth rate) from 2025–2028.

In a recent development, moving on to Sempra Energy (SRE), a utility holding company. Earlier this month, the company declared a quarterly dividend of $0.6575 per share, payable on October 15. At an annualized dividend of $2.63 per share, SRE stock offers a yield of about 3.1%.

Recently, Jefferies analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith upgraded SRE stock to Buy from Hold but slightly lowered the price target to $97 from $101. The 5-star analyst noted that Sempra stock is trading at a price/earnings multiple that is 14% below its electric peers due to concerns about Texas transmission capital expenditure and the failure of California legislation.

Smith noted that the derating of weaker California peers PG&E (PCG) and Edison International (EIX) is weighing on the sum-of-the-parts (SOTP) valuation but is becoming less relevant given their materially higher fire risk compared to Sempra Energy.

Quad9 pulled their DNS service from France
