💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best all-in-one printer should make everyday jobs simpler, whether you're printing shipping labels, scanning crucial paperwork, copying forms or producing color photos at home.
  • Our tested picks cover each of those needs, from the Canon Color imageCLASS MF753Cdw II being a capable all-rounder for most households to low-cost options like the Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW.
  • Industry observers note that at Tom's Guide, we test each printer for printing speeds, print quality, ink costs and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best all-in-one printer should make everyday jobs simpler, whether you're printing shipping labels, scanning crucial paperwork, copying forms or producing color photos at home. The right choice depends on what you print and how often: some models prioritise rapid document handling, while others keep ink costs down or deliver stronger photo output.

Our tested picks cover each of those needs, from the Canon Color imageCLASS MF753Cdw II being a capable all-rounder for most households to low-cost options like the Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW. There's even the Inkwon Tag, a compact creative printer for stickers and creating custom T-shirts.

Industry observers note that at Tom's Guide, we test each printer for printing speeds, print quality, ink costs and more. Read on to find the model that best matches your workload, budget and must-have features, including scanning, copying and faxing.

Printers might not be the most impressive (or interesting) things in the world, but they are supremely useful. To make sure you get the best printer possible, our dedicated reviews team put printers through their paces. That's going to be Nikita Achanta, on the Tom's Guide side, who's been testing consumer electronics for years. Then there are our freelancers, such as Eric Butterfield, who's tested a range of brands.

These are the tests that we put the printers through so that we can properly evaluate their performance.

It has been revealed that with the amount of shipping labels I need printed and documents that need copying for my household, a printer has become a quiet essential for my home. That's why I wanted a simple, do-it-all machine, and I refer to our experts, Nikita Achanta and Eric Butterfield, for all the in-depth recommendations they have to offer.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

According to recent reports, when it comes down to it, the Canon Color imageCLASS MF753Cdw II is quite simply the only printer you'll ever need. Yes, it can print, scan, copy and fax, but it does it all with a hassle-free setup experience and rapid speeds across the board. When a printer actually gives easy step-by-step instructions on how to fix a paper jam, you know it's a good one.

In our tests, it delivered a five-page text print job in just 11.31 seconds (26.5 pages per minute) and scanned in color in 6.22 seconds, and that's faster than its inkjet competitors.

And this 250-capacity printer (plus an extra 150 prints in the middle section) has quick start-up, too, as our reviewer, Nikita, found it effortless to get up and running, with warm-up times as quick as 14 seconds from off.

It has been revealed that it isn't just speed, as print quality is consistently sharp and detailed, both in color and black and white, and everyday jobs came out looking just as sharp as they did on our screens. Where the MF753Cdw II pulls ahead of inkjet competitors like the more budget-friendly Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 is in raw speed and features.

You get much faster printing and a true all-in-one experience (there's no faxing on the G3290), but running costs are higher if you print in volume. Against the business-class Epson EcoTank Pro ET-5850, the MF753Cdw II still keeps up on print speed and quality but can’t match those rock-bottom ink costs.

That’s the main compromise here: the per-page price is higher than what you’ll find with most ink tank printers (around 5.1 cents per color page and 2.7 cents per mono print). But not by that much, and that shouldn't put you off grabbing this workhorse.

If you want a dependable, fuss-free machine for everyday tasks — letters, homework, invoices, you name it — the MF753Cdw II is the best fit for most households.

Unless you need faxing in your life, this is the all-in-one printer to grab if you're after a reliable machine for excellent prints. The Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW stands out largely thanks to its exceptionally low ink costs: just 0.3 cents per black page and 0.94 cents per color page based on our lab testing. That's value you can't ignore.

It has been revealed that in daily use, the T780DW keeps pace with demanding routines. It prints standard text documents at 12.4 pages per minute (ppm) and handles double-sided text at 6.7 ppm. These speeds put it among the fastest inkjets we've tested for both single and duplex jobs, making it reliable for everything from schoolwork to business invoices.

Print and scan quality are equally reassuring. In our hands-on tests, text and graphics came out crisp and accurate, while color scans preserved detail and clarity.

Industry observers note that the main compromise is its 20-sheet automatic document feeder. While fine for light multi-page copying and scanning, if you've got a large batch of documents, it will take some time to do. That, and there's no USB thumb drive port, and don't expect to make double-sided copies or scans via the automatic document feeder (ADF).

In any case, for those who want low running costs and easy printing, the Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW will fit in nicely with your home or office.

According to recent reports, whether you're a photographer or just need highly detailed, colorful prints, the Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 is the all-in-one printer for you. Sure, it may come with fewer additional features, but it excels where it matters: print quality and affordability.

Sources indicate that it's a modest printer; it has just one paper tray and no document feeder, and it's not the speediest option. But for home use, it's an excellent choice. Expect this to deliver reliable, high-quality prints with the versatility to do documents, photos and double-sided print jobs. Speaking of which, those graphic prints and glossy photos will come out with plenty of detail and natural, accurate colors.

Sources indicate that while the Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 prints at pretty average speeds, it actually excels at double-sided documents. In our testing, it printed single-sided pages at an average of 9.2 pages per minute, but double-sided text documents cranked up to 7.2 pages per minute, the fastest duplex print speed we've recorded of any recent ink tank printers.

And thanks to its easy setup process, robust wireless support (this thing can print via Wi-Fi or a smartphone app) and low ink costs (we estimate color prints cost roughly 0.9 cents per page, significantly lower than the 1.9 cents per page category average), I recommend the Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 for anyone seeking an affordable, reliable ink all-in-one printer, especially for photo printing.

If your at-home office needs fast, reliable color printing day in and day out, the Epson EcoTank Pro ET-5850 is just the printer you'll want. In our tests, it handled a six-page mixed color document in just 1 minute and 8 seconds (5.3 pages per minute), nearly doubling the category average, so you won’t be waiting on significant print jobs during busy stretches.Where the ET-5850 really stands out for speedy work prints is its speed with graphics-heavy jobs. Letter-size glossy photos print in 2 minutes and 21 seconds, far outpacing typical inkjets. The three separate paper input trays mean you can keep letter, legal, and specialty papers ready to go, which helps minimize interruptions if multiple people are printing different document types.

Recent findings suggest that moreover, you're getting an impressively low ink costs with a device capable of handling more than 3,000 pages per month. During our testing, we found an extremely low per-page cost of 0.4 cents for text pages, and 1.6 cents per color page. The printer can scan, copy and fax, uses dual 250-page paper cassettes and has a 50-sheet automatic document feeder.

Recent findings suggest that setup was mostly straightforward, but we did run into some hiccups. Connecting to our network required manually entering a router password (WPS isn’t supported), and the touchscreen flagged network problems before resolving. Once added, using the printer with a Mac was simple, but it’s worth noting you might spend extra time on initial setup and troubleshooting.If you’re after an all-in-one that keeps pace with high-volume, graphics-rich business tasks and want flexible paper handling, the ET-5850 is a great fit.

It has been revealed that alright, this one's a little different from any other all-in-one printer, as the Inkwon Tag is a one-of-a-kind portable color inkjet printer. Instead of printing, scanning or copying documents, this pocketable printer delivers all the fun stuff — instant photo prints for scrapbooks, heat transfers for creating custom T-shirts, temporary tattoos and even stickers.

This 4-in-1 portable printer is as tiny as it is light, coming in at 4.1 x 3.8 x 1.7 inches and weighing just 8.2 ounces. Our reviewer, Nikita, has no problems carrying this around in a pocket, as it's actually smaller than the best massive phones around today.

In a recent development, despite its size, you'll find it boasts surprisingly good print quality, no matter the image. It uses a CMY three-dye-based ink system (no dedicated black ink, though) with a resolution of 600 dpi, making it excellent for small prints of friends and loved ones, designs of your choosing or even screenshots from games. And it's all extremely easy to use, right from setting it up to the very user-friendly app for editing and printing photos.

Industry observers note that it isn't perfect, as it can only handle one sheet of paper at a time, and don't expect it to create any borderless prints. It's also quite a pricey portable printer, coming in at $299, but its ink costs and paper refills are much more value-friendly when compared to its competition, especially from Canon or Instax (plus, those brands don't offer 4-in-1 portable printer options with sticker or heat transfer capabilities).

To have a mini, portable printer by your side to instantly create stickers to personalize whatever you want, temporary tattoos for parties, heat transfers for customized T-shirts and Polaroid-like photos, all at low running ink costs? As far as portable all-in-one printers go, the Inkwon Tag is a winner.

If you're looking for a compact, capable printer purely for stickers and photo prints, then the StickerPix Print + Cut is exactly what you're after. It comes in an adorable design, is fast at printing stickers and offers loads of templates to customize what you want to print. There are only 18 sheets of sticker/photo paper out of the box, so you'll need to invest in more, and the Inkwon Tag offers a bit more "all-in-one" versatility, but the Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut is well worth grabbing for all things stickers! Read our full Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut review.

Sources indicate that (★★★★☆)The Brother INKvestment MFC-J995DW bucked the trend of printers gouging you on ink costs by coming with roughly a year's worth of ink (depending on how much you print) pre-loaded in the extra-large ink cartridges, so you get a great price-per-page right out of the gate. On top of that, the Brother INKvestment MFC-J995DW offers solid printing, scanning and copying. But this model is trickier to find these days, and more of the current Brother printers of its kind do just the job for less these days. Read our full Brother INKvestment MFC-J995DW review.

According to recent reports, (★★★★☆½)The Brother MFC-L2750DW XL is the best multifunction laser printer we've reviewed in years for everything but color prints. Every print is sharp and clean, and it's packed with features including a quick ADF, fast duplex printing and copying, fax capability, and a second paper tray. But this is one pricey machine!Read our full Brother MFC-L2750DW XL review.

It has been revealed that (★★★★☆)Looking for another photo printer option? The Canon Pixma TR8620 is a fantastic shout that offers plenty of office features, from scanning and faxing to a 20-page ADF, a duplexer for two-sided printing, and two paper trays for keeping two types of paper at the ready. But that extra ink cartridge does bump up the cost of ink. Read our full Canon Pixma TR8620 review.

According to recent reports, to help you find the best all-in-one printer, we put each model through an extensive range of printer tests, including timed prints of text, mixed text and graphics and color photos. The resulting prints are carefully examined for errors and problems, and compared with samples from other printers to determine the print quality.

We time every test print to see how rapidly the machine handles document printing, and closely examine the finished product to determine how well different printing tasks are handled.

We also test the scanning and copying functions of the printer, timing how promptly it captures a page and comparing the results to the original images to determine how well it captures color and detail.

To measure the cost of owning and operating a printer, we look at the current street price of ink refills and the estimated number of pages that each cartridge can produce, and calculate the cost of printing a single page.

Not sure which all-in-one printer to buy? Obviously, you want a printer that performs well, so all of our reviews and rankings discuss a printer's output quality and speed, but there's more to an all-in-one printer than just how quickly it can crank out documents.

In a recent development, some companies even offer subscription services that save you money while sending you ink just in time to replace that empty cartridge. Learn more in our article HP Instant Ink vs. Canon vs. Epson: Are ink subscriptions worth it?

Ink-tank printers, a type of Inkjet, usually offer the lowest running costs because their refill bottles deliver far more pages than conventional cartridges.

In our guide, the Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW is the best-value option for home or light-office use, while the Epson EcoTank Pro ET-5850 pairs very low per-page costs with the capacity and features needed for heavier business printing.

You should compare current cost-per-page figures with your expected print volume, not just the printer’s upfront price.

Choose an inkjet if you print color graphics or photos, want a lower upfront price or value the low ongoing costs of an ink-tank model. Choose a laser all-in-one if your priority is fast, sharp text documents and a responsive office workflow.

The Canon Color imageCLASS MF753Cdw II is our top pick, as it's a fast laser workhorse, whereas the Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 is the stronger fit for photo printing.

An automatic document feeder (ADF) is worthwhile if you regularly scan, copy or fax multi-page documents, as it feeds the sheets for you instead of requiring one page at a time on the scanner glass.

Recent findings suggest that it matters less for occasional household printing or photo-focused use. Also check its capacity and whether it supports double-sided scanning: an ADF does not automatically mean both sides can be scanned in one pass.

Recent findings suggest that some can, but not every all-in-one printer with an ADF supports automatic double-sided scanning or copying. Do not confuse duplex printing with duplex scanning: a printer may print on both sides of a sheet while still requiring you to turn over originals when scanning or copying.

Check the model’s specifications before buying; the Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW has an ADF but does not support duplex scanning or copying through it.

In a recent development, many current all-in-one printers support wireless mobile printing through a manufacturer app, Apple AirPrint or another built-in service. The Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290, for example, supports Wi-Fi and printing through a smartphone app.

Before buying, confirm that the printer works with your phone or tablet, operating system, preferred app and network setup. Some features may require the device and printer to be on the same Wi-Fi network.

Apple is wrapping up a packed year for newly introduced products, but there are already several 2027 releases I’m very excited for. Here are my current most anticipated new products rumored for next year.

The iPhone’s 20th anniversary is rumored to bring a special upcoming model that’s been dubbed ‘iPhone 20 Pro.’.

iPhone 20 Pro is expected to introduce a fresh design inspired by the iPhone Air, reintroducing curves and possibly titanium, and with a quad-curved display that wraps around the edges for a bezel-free appearance.

Industry observers note that I recently decided the iPhone Duo wasn’t the right model for me. Because HomeView has been a hit for us, I’m eager to see how Apple evolves and expands it with the rumored ‘HomeView Ultra’ with a 9-inch screen that can automatically rotate 360° to face whoever’s speaking.

Mostly though, the idea of a HomeView that automatically rotates to face you sounds really useful. There’s a spot in my kitchen that would be perfect for kitchen and dining room use if the screen could swivel automatically.

The Apple Watch Series 13 might introduce an overhauled design, with one leaker claiming it will break compatibility of watch bands.

In a recent development, I’m tempering my expectations for this, since plenty of Apple Watch redesign rumors have come and gone with little actual change. But Mark Gurman has hinted we might get a redesigned Watch next year too. And after years of the same basic look, I’m fascinated to see what the next generation of Apple Watch design could be.

I’m very happy with my Apple Watch Series 12, and it’s becoming even more powerful with watchOS 27.3. But it’s very much an revision focused on internals, so if Apple does deliver an external overhaul, the latest Watch will merit its spot among my most anticipated products list.

Which new Apple products are you most hoping for or anticipating for 2027? Let us know in the comments.

These are the best mesh Wi-Fi systems we've tested to say goodbye to Wi-Fi dead zones

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tired of Wi-Fi drops throughout your home?
  • According to recent reports, at Tom's Guide, we put each mesh Wi-Fi system through real-world scenarios, from multi-story homes to outdoor use.
  • Sources indicate that for the best mesh Wi-Fi system you can buy today, we recommend the MSI Roami BE Pro for reliable speeds and long-distance coverage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tired of Wi-Fi drops throughout your home? The best mesh Wi-Fi systems can eliminate internet dead zones and turn your house into a powerhouse for connectivity, no matter how far away devices are from a router. To prove it, we've done the testing to help you find the right mesh system.

According to recent reports, at Tom's Guide, we put each mesh Wi-Fi system through real-world scenarios, from multi-story homes to outdoor use. This allows us to see how fast internet speeds are at multiple ranges, especially through objects and walls. So, if you've been struggling to get a strong Wi-Fi signal across your home, the mesh Wi-Fi systems we recommend will help you sort that problem out.

Sources indicate that for the best mesh Wi-Fi system you can buy today, we recommend the MSI Roami BE Pro for reliable speeds and long-distance coverage. This Wi-Fi 7 mesh system will take you far for its price, but there are more options we've tested for homes.

According to recent reports, soon, you'll see more of the next standard of mesh Wi-Fi systems arrive with Wi-Fi 8. We've already tested the first Wi-Fi 8 router, but there's no need to rush to get this yet, as there aren't any consumer devices that can take advantage of it. In the meantime, we have even more mesh systems worth considering!

According to recent reports, for the latest wireless connectivity, or to cover your home on a budget, this guide will help you find the best mesh Wi-Fi system for your needs, with in-depth reviews and test results. Let's dive in.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The MSI Roamii BE Pro isn't the fastest around, nor does it deliver the longest range, but it excels at speeds, distances and setup for half the price of other tri-band WiFi 7 routers. That's why it's the best mesh Wi-Fi system we recommend for most, especially if you're looking for an affordable way to upgrade to Wi-Fi 7.

According to recent reports, the Roamii BE Pro immediately stands out for its real-world speed across a whole house, reaching 1.885 Gbps at 15 feet and still delivering 66.3 Mbps at a distant 90 feet. That kind of consistent performance means you won’t be left hunting for a signal in the farthest room.

In our testing, the Roamii BE Pro also excelled at mid-range distances, recording 815.2 Mbps at 50 feet — a result that puts it squarely among the fastest mesh systems we’ve seen.

It has been revealed that we found it outpaces the TP-Link Deco BE23 at close range (1.885 Gbps vs. 1.449 Gbps), but its real advantage is balancing those speeds with broader coverage, a feat some rivals like the Netgear Orbi 870 only match at longer distances. That makes the Roamii BE Pro a better pick for anyone who wants both fast speeds and reliable whole-home coverage, not just one or the other.

See our speed measurements tested at different distances.

In a recent development, during two weeks of everyday use, the Roamii BE Pro kept up without breaking a sweat. That includes streaming 4K video, downloading large files, gaming and emailing.

It has been revealed that plus, wired device fans get a trio of 2.5 Gbps LAN ports and a USB 3.0 port. It's just a shame that this isn't available in single or three-packs, meaning you'd have to buy another two-pack if you're looking to add more nodes. At least it isn't too pricey!

According to recent reports, setup is a breeze: after scanning the QR code, entering a network name and updating the firmware, I had both nodes running in just 15 minutes. If you want the quickest path to reliable, top-tier Wi-Fi 7 speeds without fuss, the Roamii BE Pro is the system to beat.

In a recent development, the TP-Link Deco BE23 shows that high-speed, Wi-Fi 7 connectivity in a mesh system doesn't have to cost you a premium. For as low as $180, you can get a set of three powerful mesh networking devices that offer up far-reaching connectivity with some absolutely amazing speeds.

Industry observers note that each of the BE23 units comes in a neat, discreet design that can be placed anywhere while hiding in plain sight, and you can set up a connection for the whole house easily with TP-Link’s Deco app. Plus, any of the units can be used as a host router. Once you're set up, you can take control of your connectivity and devices via the app, like integrating and controlling Tapo, Kasa, Philips Hue and Matter home automation devices.

Speed is the star of the show, especially for this mesh system's affordable price. In our testing, we saw highs of 1.449 Gbps at 15 feet, and still 150.1 Mbps as far away as 90 feet. Those numbers beat many routers we've tested, even though it understandably falls behind the likes of a tri-band system (like the TP-Link Deco BE63 with 1.821 Gbps at 15 feet away).

With a maximum range of 115 feet for each unit, this mesh system will take you far (quite literally, connectivity-wise). Now that's an excellent balance between price and performance.

What you won't get here are more advanced features, like the 6 GHz band (just 2.4GHz and 5GHz here) or a super-wide 320 MHz data channel, and there's only a pair of 2.5 Gbps networking ports without a USB port, which makes wired connections limited.

In a recent development, for an affordable way to keep your whole home connected with fantastic internet speeds, the price is right with the TP-Link Deco BE23. It may not be the fastest or the most advanced, but for value, it's hard to go wrong with this mesh setup.

The Netgear Orbi 870 is a powerful mesh Wi-Fi system that really excels at medium and long ranges, even outperforming its larger, more expensive older sibling.

Despite its more premium price, I really like the more cylindrical design with a cleaner overall look of the Orbi 870 and the rest of the manufacturer’s Wi-Fi 7-powered mesh kits. While you’ll often see it in white at online retailers, you can actually get an all-black version too, but only on Netgear’s site.

Recent findings suggest that the Orbi 870 is a very reliable and feature-packed mesh Wi-Fi system that’s ideal for futureproofing your home network thanks to its slew of multi-gig ports, including a 10 Gbps input. In his testing, Brian saw speeds of 1.82 Gbps at close range (15 feet).

According to recent reports, however, it was the Orbi 870’s mid- and long-range performance that impressed him the most. For instance, at 50 and 75 feet, this mesh Wi-Fi system had download speeds of over 600 Mbps, beating both the entry-level Orbi 770 and even the Orbi 970 at the top of Netgear’s mesh lineup.

Sources indicate that even at a distance of 90 feet from Brian’s test laptop, it was at just over 100 Mbps, while the Orbi 970 and even TP-Link’s Deco BE85 were under 50 Mbps. At launch, a two-pack cost $1,000 (though you can often find it cheaper now), so the Orbi 870 is certainly an investment, just like the rest of the devices in Netgear’s Orbi line.

According to recent reports, however, if you have a large home you want to fill with a strong Wi-Fi signal and a top-tier multi-gig internet plan, it could definitely be worth it. Just keep in mind that you will need to set aside some extra cash if you want to secure your home network with it using Netgear’s Armor security package or want extended technical support, as only 90 days are included.

The Acer Predator Connect T7 is a mesh Wi-Fi system with a heavy focus on gamers. However, unlike my previous mesh router pick for gaming, the Asus ROG Rapture GT6, it’s a Wi-Fi 7-powered device with a much more subtle look.

Instead of RGB and lots of logos, the Predator Connect T7 features a taller, rectangular design in white or black, and at first glance, it looks quite similar to an Xbox Series X. There’s a splash of RGB lighting on the top, but this mesh kit has a sleeker and more restrained look that I think definitely works in its favor.

Just like with the best gaming routers, the Predator Connect T7 has a low-latency design that uses Intel’s Killer Prioritization engine for peak gaming performance. It also comes with free built-in security software and makes full use of all of Wi-Fi 7’s best features.

During testing, Brian saw download speeds of 1.9 Gbps at close range (15 feet) with good mid-range performance. While the Predator Connect T7 has a multi-gig input port, its wired Ethernet ports are limited to gigabit speeds, so plugging in one of the best gaming laptops won’t give you a significant speed boost over connecting via Wi-Fi.

The Acer Predator Connect T7 is one of the few mesh Wi-Fi systems specifically designed for gamers and if you want a mesh router that looks as slick as your gaming PC, it’s a substantial step up from the Asus ROG Rapture GT7 (which superseded the GT6 we used to recommend).

It has been revealed that however, it is on the expensive side at $330 per device, and unlike other mesh kits, you won’t see any discounts at all when buying a multi-pack. Still, if you want gaming-level network performance with the added benefits of mesh and want something less flashy, the Predator Connect T7 is an excellent mesh Wi-Fi system and the only one for gamers with Wi-Fi 7 support so far.

Recent findings suggest that the Eero Pro 7 is a smaller and sleeker mesh Wi-Fi system that’s incredibly simple to set up and use. Unlike Eero’s past mesh kits, which had a puck-shaped design, this one has a rounded rectangular shape and, at 7.1 x 5.8 x 2.6 inches, you won’t have any trouble finding a place for it and its satellites around your home.

In a recent development, after testing the larger, more powerful Eero Max 7 myself, I really like the Pro 7’s more compact design and the fact that it's significantly cheaper, too. The biggest selling point of the Pro 7 and Eero’s other mesh Wi-Fi systems is that even a home networking novice will have no trouble at all getting them up and running.

Setup and configuration are handled entirely through the very user-friendly Eero app. Besides how it looks, I really like the way that updates are downloaded and installed automatically, so your mesh Wi-Fi system is always running the latest software.

In his testing, Brian saw download speeds of 1.9 Gbps at close distances (15 feet), but the Pro 7 was equally impressive at mid-range distances with speeds just under a gigabit.

Industry observers note that the Eero Pro 7 does cost a bit more than the competition, but nowhere close to what you’d pay for an Orbi mesh kit. As an Amazon company, Eero works great with your Alexa-powered and other smart home devices, and you can even use an Echo Dot as a mesh extender to add some extra range to your home network.

According to recent reports, if you want a fast and capable Wi-Fi 7-powered mesh system that’s simple to set up and just works, the Eero Pro 7 is very easy to recommend, especially since it's a lot cheaper than the Max 7. The one downside is that you’re limited to just two Ethernet ports, but they are the faster 5 Gbps variety, which is great if you have a multi-gig internet plan.

Industry observers note that the TP-Link Deco BE85 is a top-of-the-line mesh Wi-Fi system that was actually the first mesh router with Wi-Fi 7 support. It builds on the cylindrical design of the Deco XE75 with a more refined and polished look, but it packs in a ton of multi-gig and even a USB port.

In a recent development, as someone who upgraded to fiber internet, I love how it has its own SFP+ port, which lets you plug your fiber line directly in at the back instead of into a separate ONT box first. Even if you’re still using one of the best cable modems, though, the Deco BE85 is a powerful mesh Wi-Fi system that won’t disappoint when it comes to performance.

Industry observers note that one thing that’s really convenient about this mesh kit and TP-Link’s other Deco devices is that they’re all identical out of the box and you can use any of them as your main router. The manufacturer’s Deco app also makes setup and configuration very easy, and in my experience, it’s on par with Eero’s app in terms of usability.

15 feet (Toms Guide): TP-Link Deco BE85 scores 1.736.

50 feet (Toms Guide): TP-Link Deco BE85 scores 790.4.

75 feet (Toms Guide): TP-Link Deco BE85 scores 179.2.

90 feet (Toms Guide): TP-Link Deco BE85 scores 42.6.

According to recent reports, during testing, Brian saw download speeds of 1.73 Gbps at a close distance (15 feet) and good mid-range speeds, too. While this might seem a bit low for a premium mesh Wi-Fi system, Brian was one of the first people to get and review the Deco BE85. It's possible this has improved with firmware updates since its launch.

The Deco BE85 has come down in price since it debuted, but it’s still expensive, even though this model does go on sale quite frequently. However, if you have a fast, multi-gig fiber internet plan and want top-notch Wi-Fi 7 performance, this mesh router is the only one I’ve seen yet with an SFP+ port on the back.

It’s worth noting that, just like with Eero, all TP-Link Deco devices are compatible with one another, so you could always mix and match or upgrade to a more powerful model later on if you need to.

Recent findings suggest that the mesh Wi-Fi systems we've used all come with amazing speeds, and we've done the testing to show how fast a router is at short and long ranges. But you'll find some will perform better at various distances, even if one delivers the fastest speeds around.

As an example, the Acer Predator Connect T7 offers the fastest speeds at 15 feet, but it loses out to the likes of the TP-Link Deco BE23 and others at 90 feet. It comes down to what you prioritize: speed or range (or a balance of both!).

So, to compare each mesh Wi-Fi system across the range of distances we've tested, check out the versus table below to help you make the right choice for your home.

Select a mesh Wi-Fi system to compare internet speed at different distances (measured in Gbps and Mbps).

According to recent reports, we test every mesh Wi-Fi system to measure performance and range, using Keysight IxChariot. Testing is done in a multi-story home with brick walls. When we test standard routers, we look at performance at a distance to provide real-world information about coverage and speeds. In addition to lab testing, we evaluate the ease of setup and features of each device, too.

We measure performance at a 15-foot distance without obstructions, so that we can gauge the maximum amount of data that a router can move. Higher throughput will serve you better in data-heavy uses, like streaming video, gaming, or connecting multiple users at once.

Range measures the furthest usable distance for a particular router. Longer ranges are better for larger homes, where rooms are spread out at a distance. We measure how much data a router can move at 15, 50, 75 and 90 feet, as well as the maximum coverage area of a mesh Wi-Fi system.

Sources indicate that we also test how well each mesh Wi-Fi system transmits and receives signals through drywall, brick, concrete and even metal walls, and how each handles coverage in a two- or three-story home. They also go through additional testing to see how well each system does when sending a signal through the main router and through the included satellites.

Of course (and most importantly), we also consider what you really get for your money, considering which features are worthwhile and how any given product compares with other devices from competing manufacturers.

According to recent reports, A lot of factors come into choosing the mesh Wi-Fi system that will suit your space, from the coverage you need to the speeds you demand — all for the right price. We've got just the tips to make your choice easier.

It has been revealed that wi-Fi 8 is currently still in the early stages of being supported on all devices, so you won't be able to take advantage of the new connectivity standard right now. Currently, no consumer devices support Wi-Fi 8 coverage, and we're not expecting to see support until sometime in 2027 or 2028.

Industry observers note that we've reviewed the first Wi-Fi 8 router, the Asus ROG Rapture GT-BN98 Pro, and are impressed by its incredible Wi-Fi speeds and range. However, we couldn't see its full potential since we're still waiting for Wi-Fi 8 hardware. We'll have to see how well mesh Wi-Fi systems with Wi-Fi 8 perform, too.

According to recent reports, while Wi-Fi 8 isn't worth getting right now, it may be worth it to many looking to future-proof their homes once more devices adopt Wi-Fi 8. Besides, it's backwards compatible with Wi-Fi 7, Wi-Fi 6 and so on. We'll keep you updated in the meantime.

Sources indicate that yes, a mesh Wi-Fi system can go through walls. Because Wi-Fi uses radio waves, these waves can pass through solid materials like walls to connect to a device.

Industry observers note that however, when Wi-Fi meets a wall, some of it goes through, some bounces off and some is absorbed. Because of this, the signal can be weaker, especially when more walls are in the way.

A mesh Wi-Fi system has an advantage in getting past this. Instead of using one router to get a signal, a mesh system uses multiple nodes placed throughout a home to bypass hard objects or walls in order to get an unobstructed signal. This means there are fewer barriers to getting a clear Wi-Fi signal.

The main downside of using a mesh Wi-Fi system is that it can be very expensive, especially compared to traditional Wi-Fi routers. These are only needed for those living in large homes or for anyone who needs Wi-Fi coverage over a long distance. For those in smaller spaces, this is overkill.

Since mesh systems come in a multi-pack of nodes, this bumps up the price, as these extra devices deliver a better range of coverage throughout a space compared to other routers.

Nodes also must be placed close enough to catch a strong signal, which can be tricky in a home with many rooms separated by concrete or brick walls. Plus, with this signal hopping between multiple nodes, there may be an increase in latency, which isn't ideal for competitive gameplay.

Otherwise, the best mesh Wi-Fi systems try to overcome these downsides, and these are still the best option to upgrade your home network wirelessly.

Recent findings suggest that mesh Wi-Fi systems come with nodes and are usually available in two-packs or three-packs, but deciding which one to get depends on the size of your home. If you live in a small or medium house, then a two-pack will usually do the trick. For large homes with more than three bedrooms or multiple stories, a three-pack is the better choice, as this will ensure that your Wi-Fi signal reaches every corner and even upstairs.

The great thing about mesh Wi-Fi systems, though, is that you can always start small and work up to something bigger. For instance, if you buy a two-pack and find that you’re still dealing with Wi-Fi dead zones in certain parts of your home, you can always add another node later to improve your coverage.

Sources indicate that plug-in Wi-Fi extenders aren’t nearly as advanced or as powerful as the nodes in a mesh Wi-Fi system. The other major problem with Wi-Fi extenders is that most of them create a separate network you have to manually switch to each time you want to use them. For instance, let’s say you put a Wi-Fi extender in your bedroom. Whenever you want to get online in that particular room, you’ll have to switch from your main Wi-Fi network to the extender, which gets annoying really fast.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, with a mesh Wi-Fi system, the nodes are all part of your main network and no switching is required. As you move from one side of your house to the other, your mesh system automatically hands off your connection to whatever satellite you’re closest to, which ensures you have a strong signal and a good connection wherever you are in your home.

As someone who's been working from home for the past eight years, Anthony Spadafora has tried everything from Wi-Fi extenders to powerline adapters to get the most out of his home network, before finally upgrading to a mesh Wi-Fi system. Along the way, he's tested out loads of different routers and network configurations. Based on what he's learned, Anthony tries to highlight the critical role Wi-Fi routers play in our day-to-day lives and how a mesh network can help solve the most common connectivity problems like Wi-Fi dead spots.

It has been revealed that with experience in testing, using and evaluating wireless data from before Wi-Fi was even a word, Brian Nadel has tried out and reviewed every major router available in his home networking lab. A LAN nerd, his philosophy is to use the router the way you would, testing networking gear for ease of setup, performance, security and above all for value. The result is peace of mind when it comes to choosing the right router.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alarms are one of the most key iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a fresh volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.

Have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm? We’ve all done it. And most often for me, it’s because my alarm volume was unintentionally set to a very low level.

I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms. And in iOS 27, Apple finally has the fix—but it requires manually setting up.

Inside Settings ⇾ Sounds & Haptics, you can now set a volume for alarms that’s independent from the systemwide ringtone setting.

Recent findings suggest that iOS 27 has two upcoming sections in this Settings screen: Alarms and Timers, and Alerts and System Sounds. Both include ‘Match Ringtone Volume’ toggles that are on by default. This means your volume for alarms, timers, alerts, and other system sounds are all determined by the ringtone volume.

But if you disable the Alarms and Timers toggle, you’ll get a upcoming volume slider that applies only to those system functions, and won’t be impacted by your ringtone volume.

As seen above, this means you can crank the Alarms and Timers volume up to the maximum level without making every other system sound, including notifications and phone calls, be similarly deafening.

So the next time you sleep through your alarm, it won’t be because the alarm was too quiet.

In case you missed it, iOS 26 introduced a welcome feature that lets you set custom snooze durations for alarms, and also an option to have alarms trigger on your iPhone even if you’re wearing an Apple Watch.

According to recent reports, do you plan to set a custom volume setting for alarms in iOS 27? Let us know in the comments.

When buying a cheap camera, you’re naturally going to have to sacrifice a few things. The latest and greatest cameras simply don’t come cheap. Usually, you’ll either have to accept an older model, or sacrifice features.

However, you absolutely don’t have to sacrifice quality. You can pick up some great cameras for well under $100, and they aren’t just cheap crap. And that’s where we come in! This guide is designed to help you filter out the cameras that are cheap, yet still great quality and built to last.

The specific features you need to look for will depend on what you’re using the camera for. If you want to take really nice photos and grow as a photographer, then you’ll want a camera with a larger sensor, decent megapixel count and good autofocus — that means you’ll need to splash out on a DSLR or mirrorless camera.

Shooting video? You’ll want 4K footage, decent stabilization and the ability to connect external microphones. A vlogging camera is ideal, or an action camera if you’ll be shooting outdoors or in extreme environments. If you’re after sky-high footage, then you’ll want a drone (and yes, you can absolutely pick up great drones without breaking the bank).

Want to print your photos? You have a few options. The high-resolution sensors in mirrorless cameras will yield the best results when printing digital images. If you want the film look, you can go for an instant camera, which will be best for immediate printing and documenting social events, or a film camera, which will produce higher quality prints but requires film to be developed.

Industry observers note that if you need a camera for travel, then it’s all about portability. You’ll want something that takes decent photos, but is small enough to fit in a pocket or backpack, and which won’t become a chore when worn around your neck.

Every single camera on this list has been through the Tom’s Guide reviews process, which means they’ve all been thoroughly tested by Tom’s Guide experts. The testing process naturally differs for the different categories of cameras — we test an action camera differently to how we test an instant camera, for example.

However, there are many things all cameras have in common. We always test how sharp the camera optics are, looking for optical distortions and image artefacts. We always evaluate how well images turn out, how detailed they are and the color accuracy of the camera. We take lots of test shots or videos with each camera, enabling us to test autofocus, exposure metering and all the extra features such as AF modes.

Sources indicate that naturally, we always evaluate the price of a product, test its build quality, and analyze both how easy the camera is to use and how sensibly it’s laid out. If there’s a smartphone app, we use it and evaluate how many extra features it adds, but also how user-friendly it is. We always evaluate the battery life of cameras, too.

In a recent development, we don’t just list the specs or features of these cameras either, and always analyze whether each of a camera’s features is good or bad, and why — that involves weighing it up against the product’s cost and competition. Throughout each review, we constantly compare each product to its rivals to help you make the most informed purchase. We’ve included links to the individual reviews for each camera within every entry, so you can get the full lowdown on each product if you want to know more.

Why spend money on even a cheap camera when you have your smartphone, right? Won't your phone take pictures just as well?

Industry observers note that that depends on the phone and indeed the camera, but generally speaking a decent dedicated camera will be able to take better photos than your smartphone. Phones have small image sensors, as there isn't much space inside a phone case for a large sensor. The iPhone 16 uses a 1/1.29-inch sensor, which is a lot smaller than the APS-C sensor used in the Canon EOS R100. A larger sensor delivers cleaner images in low light. That said, many phones these days feature larger sensors than some cameras, especially compact cameras.

Sources indicate that another factor is optics. Smartphones have to use small lenses — again, as space is a major consideration. Smaller lenses just can't match the sharpness and quality of larger lenses on dedicated cameras, especially those on interchangeable lens cameras (like mirrorless or DSLR bodies).

It has been revealed that and while some smartphones offer manual controls, often these aren't truly manual. You can adjust "aperture" on an iPhone, for instance, but the phone simply applies a software-generated blur to approximate the look of a shallow depth of field at wide apertures. While this looks OK at a glance, study the image closely and you'll see mistakes and things blurred that shouldn't be. This reliance on software is repeated in other areas by your smartphone camera, and generally results in poorer image quality.

And finally, there's use case. If you want to shoot film photos, or print your photos instantly, you can't do either with a smartphone alone. Using a dedicated camera is often more fun, too! There's something special about the experience of using a camera that smartphones can't quite replicate.

Industry observers note that that really depends on the category of camera you need, and the definition of “cheap” changes based on said category. If you want the best image quality or a vlogging camera, you’ll need a mirrorless camera like the EOS R100, and cheap means around the $250-$400 mark. Action cameras, expect to spend around $175 - $200 for a cheap model.

Recent findings suggest that great instant cameras and compact cameras can easily be found for around the $100 mark, while affordable film cameras can be yours for very little more. If you want a cheap drone, you can expect to spend in the vicinity of $200.

In a recent development, no. Or at least, not until they're sure they want to get into photography. Cheap cameras are a great way to see if you like photography (or shooting video), and whether you really want to put in the time and dedication to learn and gain experience.

According to recent reports, that's not to say you should buy the cheapest camera you can find, though, as there are many terrible cameras out there which are a total waste of money. You should buy a decent camera which will allow you to learn without breaking the bank. And that's where this guide comes in! It will help you choose a cheap camera that's also good quality.

Tech Report: MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The biggest concern with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat.
  • MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.
  • Recent findings suggest that heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest concern with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat. It doesn’t matter if the battery specs say it can charge at Qi2.2 speeds if the heat slows it down after 15 minutes. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro directly targets heat with a built-in fan in the MagSafe battery.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Recent findings suggest that heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge. Anker’s answer in the MagGo 2 Pro is a small fan inside of it. Anker notes it keeps the charging surface below 96.8°F, and the fan adjusts its speed based on what’s plugged in and how the charge is progressing. You can switch between Cool and Silent modes if you don’t want to hear it running at all.

In a recent development, the result of having this fan is a Qi2.2 power bank that actually reaches Qi2.2 speeds for a full charge. Anker rates it at 25% on an iPhone 17 Pro in 10 minutes, then to 50% in 25 minutes, which is the kind of speed you’d normally expect from a wired charging session.

The MagGo 2 Pro battery is 10,000mAh, which is enough for a little over one full charge of an iPhone Pro Max and closer to two on a standard iPhone. Size-wise, it has about the same footprint as the iPhone itself and is roughly an ounce lighter than Anker’s standard MagGo. It’s not a slim battery, but for one with a fan, it’s workable in your travel bag, crossbody, etc.

The single USB-C port works both directions at up to 45 watts. If you plug in a 45-watt charger to it, the MagGo 2 Pro can charge from empty to 80% in under an hour. The same port will charge a Mac or an iPad up to 45 watts in a pinch, which is a nice add-on for a MagSafe battery. You are not going to charge up your MacBook Pro from zero to full with it, but it’s a nice way to get a little charge in an emergency at the airport, etc.

Sources indicate that one thing to know before you buy: the cable in the box is a 1-foot USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and Anker says that reaching the full 45-watt recharge speed requires a 45-watt-rated cable. So keep that in mind as you pack for a trip.

Industry observers note that anker put a small display on the side that cycles through six screens with a side button: charging wattage, battery percentage, battery health, and temperature. It’s a nice touch to know you are reaching the 25-watt Qi 2.2 speed.

There’s also a built-in stand that adjusts from flat to 80 degrees and folds back into the body when you’re done. You can also quickly turn off charging if you simply want to use it as a stand. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro comes in Phantom Gray, Burgundy Red, Polar Night Blue, and Starlight Silver.

In a recent development, qi2.2 is the Holy Grail of MagSafe chargers, but as I noted in the beginning, it’s irrelevant if the heat throttles it. To get full 25-watt MagSafe charging on the go, you’ll likely need something with a fan, unless you’re in colder weather. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro solves that problem with a built-in fan, a handy side display, and a stand.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro is available on Amazon and directly from Anker.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that meta’s Muse AI agent has only been around for a few months, but already has a track record of user privacy violations.
  • Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages.
  • According to a Reuters investigation, Meta employees testing Muse mentioned the agent messaged them about topics they hadn’t asked it about, including career advice, a follow-up on a request for childcare, products they hadn’t purchased, and, crucially, bank account balances they didn’t recognize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that meta’s Muse AI agent has only been around for a few months, but already has a track record of user privacy violations. Even Meta employees are reporting concerning incidents, including the agent taking actions they didn’t ask it to and sharing information they didn’t recognize that appears to belong to other users.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages.

According to a Reuters investigation, Meta employees testing Muse mentioned the agent messaged them about topics they hadn’t asked it about, including career advice, a follow-up on a request for childcare, products they hadn’t purchased, and, crucially, bank account balances they didn’t recognize.

These incidents “prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data,” Reuters stated.

Reuters stated “an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: ‘BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2,722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5,899.57.'” In another instance, Muse booked a non-refundable Airbnb for an employee who hadn’t instructed it to.

Muse notified another employee, who was using the agent on her personal phone, about a message she’d received on Signal, though she said she hadn’t given the agent access to the encrypted messaging app.

Also: Meta Muse is the worst AI agent for privacy – and I’ve tried them all.

Reuters and the AI Now Institute determined, through testing on an Android phone and a Mac, that Muse used “permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate.” Because Muse is set up with automatic access to Android push notifications, it didn’t need explicit app access to read messages.

The tests did not work on an iPhone, suggesting better protections against Muse’s prying.

It has been revealed that similarly, in September, a user reported Muse had shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before checking with him. The incident was ultimately a misunderstanding between the terms the user thought he’d consented to and how much access he was actually handing over, which exemplifies that Meta and the user may have explicitly different definitions of access, and that Muse can take advantage of that grey area.

Meta told Reuters these incidents were either isolated or the result of hallucinations, though Reuters could not confirm that.

Sources indicate that these are just the latest in a string of alarming incidents surrounding Muse. In its first month, a cybersecurity professional discovered Muse had a serious zero-day bug that made it hijackable. At least one journalist found the AI sifting through his Apple Messages after he’d explicitly denied those permissions, which Apple then issued stronger privacy protections to address. Banks have also blocked agents over concerns.

As a manufacturer, Meta doesn’t have a solid history of respecting user privacy. That legacy is partly what informed ZDNET contributor David Gewirtz’s suspicion of the AI assistant when he tested it, though it earned his assigned title of “worst AI agent for privacy” all on its own. The agent asked him for everything from contacts and chats to his logins and passwords, and Meta automatically uses conversations with Muse to train its AI.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac.

In a recent development, public awareness of the risks of AI agents hit a peak last year with the viral OpenClaw. The predominant advice for using agents has been to take every privacy precaution: Be careful with the data you share and the apps you give it permissions for, and watch what you tell it. But if users believe they’re doing so by restricting access to certain apps, just for Muse to find a way in anyway, privacy hygiene isn’t enough.

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible.

Reuters’ findings may provide an opportunity for Google’s agentic offering, now called Tasks (formerly Spark), which it made free (with usage limits, like Muse) this week.

These are the best noise canceling earbuds we've tested that are actually worth your money right now
