💡 Key Takeaways
  • True silence when you're out and about is impossible — but you can get incredibly close with some of the best noise-canceling earbuds.
  • It has been revealed that at the moment, the best noise-canceling earbuds you can buy are the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2.
  • In a recent development, if they're over your budget or you need something you won't worry about losing as much, there's always the excellent CMF By Nothing Buds 2A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

True silence when you're out and about is impossible — but you can get incredibly close with some of the best noise-canceling earbuds. Thanks to advances in active noise cancellation (ANC), they're great at keeping the noise of your commute at bay, and their in-ear design makes them super portable. But which should you buy?

It has been revealed that at the moment, the best noise-canceling earbuds you can buy are the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. They've got the best ANC we've ever tested, and offer a comfortable fit so that you can wear them for long periods of time. There's little more we'd ask.

In a recent development, if they're over your budget or you need something you won't worry about losing as much, there's always the excellent CMF By Nothing Buds 2A. They don't cost anywhere near as much, but also offer great ANC and solid sound quality.

Industry observers note that I maintain the site's buying guides for headphones, wireless earbuds, Bluetooth speakers, soundbars, and more. I have spent more than 20 years testing audio equipment for my own enjoyment, and was previously the Audio Editor here at Tom's Guide. There's nothing more I love than jamming out to my favorite tunes on audio equipment of different prices and sizes.

Industry observers note that the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 bring improvements to the formula across the board, in all but one key area. If you were to unbox your brand-new buds next to a pair of the old model, you'd be forgiven for wondering if you'd be shortchanged.

It has been revealed that they look identical. All the way down to their eartip shape and silicone fitting wing, the QuietComfort Ultra Buds family is one that has a particular style that it has stuck with for a long time.

According to recent reports, pop them in your ears and you soon notice the difference. They've got even better ANC than the old model, with some of the most impressive noise canceling around. They block out everything — I took them on a long train journey, and found that all of the noise of my carriage was completely unnoticeable, even when not listening to music. It's like magic, as the orchestral sound swells and the noise disappears.

Sources indicate that the transparency mode is very good as well, and it works well if you want to order your breakfast when you're going to work. The touch controls work well, and the charging case now contains a wireless charging coil so that you can more easily keep them fully charged.

Recent findings suggest that battery life is still not the best, though. Six hours with ANC on isn't quite up there, and four hours when you turn on 'immersive audio' is lackluster. It's not really worth turning the Immersive Audio setting on anyway.

It just thins out your music as it tries to distribute it around an artificially extended soundstage, and uses up an extra two hours of battery life. The soundstage is wide enough as it is, and the sound improved over the first model for some great audio as well.

According to recent reports, they're still the best ANC buds you can get your hands on, and the Gen 2 just cemented their place in the annals of earbuds history. That ANC is just so good.

Industry observers note that with the AirPods Pro 3, Apple was looking to unseat Bose's buds from the top of the list. Unfortunately for Apple, Bose released the refreshed Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 just before the latest AirPods hit shelves, but the AirPods Pro 3 are still a significant step up over their predecessors.

According to recent reports, they've got sound to match the XM5, with a similarly natural sound profile and some extra juicy features that make them a whole lot more usable than the majority of the other options. They're a great jack of all trades and perfect for iPhone people.

The ANC is, Apple tells us, "2x as good as the AirPods Pro 2". In our testing, we've found that the ANC is, indeed, much better than the ANC of the previous models. It's better at blocking out sounds across the frequency spectrum, although it still focuses on the sounds you'll hear in your day-to-day life.

According to recent reports, that means that bus journeys are more comfortable and office stays more tolerable. The transparency mode is natural-sounding as well and gives you more battery life.

According to recent reports, there are some extra features on board the AirPods Pro 3. There's a heart rate monitor and Live Translation, although we found these to be novelty extras as opposed to 'reasons to buy.'.

It has been revealed that there are meaningful improvements in some other key areas, however. Fit is far better, and it seals very well in the ear to help the ANC. The battery life is excellent, with 2 hours more than the previous model, bringing them up to par with the Sony earbuds.

There are a couple of drawbacks. Android users won't like their less impressive features for their OS, but you were probably eyeing up the buds from Sony and Bose. There's still only one color option — white — and I've got AirPods that have died permanently gray after spending too much time in my black jeans pocket.

The AirPods Pro 3 are still an excellent pair of buds for iPhone customers, however, and some of the best ANC buds around.

There are good budget buds, but there are very few as impressive as the CMF By Nothing Buds 2A. If you weren’t already aware, CMF is Nothing's most affordable product range, and the 2A sit at the bottom price rung of the brand's earbud lineup.

You might have thought that such a low price would mean low-quality ANC — but no, that’s far from the truth. The CMF Buds (sorry CMF, I’m not typing “by Nothing” every time) 2A are a budget revelation when it comes to keeping unwanted noise at bay.

In a recent development, we found that the sound of buses and other public transport was blocked very well by the buds, making sure that your commute is more comfortable. It’s adaptive as well, changing and shifting depending on the ambient noise levels.

According to recent reports, transparency mode was great when we wanted to order some lunch, with clear sound when we were chatting with the service staff. It’s not quite up there with the AirPods Pro 3 or the Sony WF-1000XM6, but then you could buy nearly ten pairs of these for the same price as either of those.

It has been revealed that they’re comfortable too, with loads of fitting options in the box so that you can dial them in according to your specific fitting preferences. The battery life is solid with 35 hours on tap — that’s plenty to get you through a week's worth of work and commuting. Multi-point makes sure you can connect to different devices without the need to dip into the settings menu, and it works well.

In a recent development, they’re obviously not perfect — some compromises have been made to keep the price down. They feel a bit cheap, and there’s no auto-pause when you take them in and out of your ears. But again, when you consider the price, the few cons are very easy to forgive.

Sound is impressive, and there are loads of extra features in the Nothing X app like a customizable EQ. We love the CMF Buds 2A, and we think you will too once you’ve got the $30 wonders in your pocket — and you want to keep the noise of your busy 7:30 AM train at bay.

Sony has been trying to take the ANC fight to Bose since the latter released its finest, and sometimes Sony has come out on top. In this case, though, it’s the runner-up — but it's so close. There are still key reasons to pick up the WF-1000XM6 instead of the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2.

But about that ANC; it’s very good. We tested the buds in a range of different environments, from the office, a train, a busy city, and more. The noise cancellation kept out just about everything, and didn’t affect the sound of the music we were listening to.

According to recent reports, it loses out to the QuietComfort in the smoothness of the delivery. That means that changes in environments are handled slightly more roughly than Boses pair, with a little noise leaking in before the algorithm takes notice. To be clear — it’s so close. If you don’t try both, you won’t notice. Side by side though, there is an edge to the Sony that’s not present in the Bose buds.

Sources indicate that the sound, though, is better than Bose’s buds. There’s more delicacy up top, and they’re less low-end heavy. Sony’s tuning is more pleasing to our ears across a range of different genres, making them a better bet for the sound-quality-conscious. The AirPods Pro 3 sound even better, though.

They’re comfortable too, with a solid range of different tips for different ear shapes. The buds themselves a slightly strange shape, and the case is a dumb shape (it's covered with angles, so it’s less comfortable to fit in a pocket than the lovely smooth Bose and Apple options), but this is still a stylish and comfy pair of wireless earbuds.

It has been revealed that battery life is… fine. It’s unimproved from the previous model, the WF-1000XM5, with around 8 hours of use with ANC turned on. That’s more than the Bose buds and around the same as the AirPods Pro 3. Still, we’d like to see more battery life from flagship earbuds, considering how much you get with more budget buds.

So in the end, it all comes down to a couple of things. If you want the best noise canceling, buy the Bose earbuds. If you want something with great ANC that works with an iPhone, then get the AirPods Pro 3. If you want something that works well with everything, offers great ANC and excellent sound quality, then pick the Sony WF-1000XM6.

In a recent development, the Noble Fokus Amadeus bring a certain class to proceedings. They're covered in a very regal red colorway, and the buds themselves have a resin finish that makes them look almost like jewelry. And I love them.

They're super comfortable, especially if you use the flanged eartips. Those will also make your ANC better, and it was already really good. It blocked out the fan in my office, and makes bus journeys and train trips a whole lot more tolerable. It's not quite up there with the Bose ANC, but it does get close to the Sony XM series. That's impressive, especially given that Noble is a much smaller company.

It has been revealed that the sound is the best bit, though. Slip them into your ears, and you're treated to the very best audio experience this side of $400. The highs are incredibly detailed, the mids are incredible, and the bass is impactful. They sound excellent — hence why they're on the list.

They lack some of the features of the competition, like the Spatial Audio of the AirPods and 360 reality audio you'll find on Sony buds, but they more than make up for it thanks to their incredible sound.

For audiophiles looking for their portable audio fix, the Noble Fokus Amadeus are the buds for you.

Fitness buds are a dime a dozen, with plenty of options available should you want to listen to music while you work out. The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the latest buds from Apple's subsidiary, and they also happen to be the best buds for fitness fanatics. They've got a useful fitting hook on each bud, and then heart rate monitors to make sure they stay in place.

In a recent development, the noise canceling, as you'd hope, is excellent. I found it perfect for most different settings, be that a quiet office or a bustling train. I'm not known for my exercise, however, so I spoke to someone who is — and what they thought of the noise canceling on board.

They took them for months of long running sessions and other fitness work, and found they blocked noise very well. Gyms silenced, annoying traffic brought to nothing. If you want to make sure your jogs, cycling, or even your swimming is distraction-free, then the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the buds for you.

According to recent reports, I was also very impressed with the battery life of the buds. According to Beats, there are 10 hours of ANC on battery life out of the buds, and my testing proved that to be pretty much spot on. That extends to 45 hours when you put them back in the (very large) charging case, for some of the best battery life in the segment. It will depend on volume level and even genre, but expect good staying power.

Sound does trip up slightly. They've got plenty of detail and some fairly dynamic bass, but there's an unfortunate cut-off in the lower mids that takes some of the edge out of your music. For most people, it's not going to be a problem. But if you're picky about how your music sounds, you may be better off with a different pair of earbuds.

The heart rate monitor is useful if you want to track more of your fitness metrics, but we found that it wasn't the most accurate. Not a massive glitch, but one worth noting.

In the end, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are a solid ANC option for everyone, but they're particularly good for those looking for a fitness companion.

Sources indicate that samsung’s buds have never topped best lists, but they’ve always had a space reserved. While they might not have the same “all things for all people” vibes as the Sony WF-1000XM6, the ultra-impressive noise canceling of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra, or the Apple user features of the AirPods line, there has been little better for users of Samsung’s phones than Samsung’s buds. They offer great performance at a slightly lower price and bring some exclusive features to the table, making them even better.

Noise-canceling-wise, you’re looking at performance that gets close to the AirPods and the Sony buds, just slotting in behind the QuietComfort Ultra. They do a great job of keeping noise at bay, as we discovered when we put them head-to-head with the Bose buds, and with music playing, you won’t find any horrible noises making their way through.

Sources indicate that transparency mode is similarly excellent, and doesn’t add the same robotic hue as cheaper buds. Perfect for when you need to speak to someone and don’t want to pop your earbuds out. In case you lose them. The algorithms that Samsung uses here are very good, and there are different levels you can access with the Samsung settings app and a separate Samsung earbuds application you can install.

Sound-wise, they’re very good as well, bringing plenty of bass and richness to the table. They’re a “major” sounding earbud, with plenty of depth. They’re similarly lovely in the mids department, making sure that music sounds great no matter the genre. Detail heads will miss out on some of the really high and clear stuff, but they’ll be better served by the buds from Sony. Either way, the sound is top-notch, even if it does focus on different parts of the frequency range.

It has been revealed that battery life is solid as a rock, although not quite as special as the likes of the Apple or Sony buds. Seven hours of staying power is plenty to get you through the work day, especially if you charge them in the case over your lunch break. The 30 hours of life in the case is actually better than the competition, which is always good, and makes sure they’re not going to need a wall outlet as often.

According to recent reports, AI features are going to be useful for some and less so for others. Still, the likes of Interpreter and others are fun extras, even if you do have to have a Samsung device for them to work properly. If you’re looking for the perfect accompaniment to your S23 or newer, then the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are the way to go.

Recent findings suggest that wired earbuds are back, and there’s no bigger sign than Bose’s noise-canceling version of the format. It’s not the first time that Bose has made wired earbuds with ANC inside, but this version brings the latest algorithms to the table for excellent ANC performance paired with a reliable, tethered connection. They’re good to, although it seems that Bose is keeping some stuff back for either the more expensive wired option or to account for a lack of a dedicated power source for the mics and tech needed for ANC.

Industry observers note that the ANC is good. Very good, in fact — we found that it blocked plenty of noise when walking down a street or working in a busy office. If you’ve not experienced the likes of the upper ANC echelons, these are going to be perfectly serviceable for everyday use. They’re just a little weaker than some of the other options on this list, with some higher sounds making their way through the barrier.

Sources indicate that transparency works well enough, making sure that you can hear what's going on the other side of the buds without all the extra noise around you. It does affect the sound of the buds slightly, however, so you’ll pay the price in sound quality when you’re ordering your McDonald's breakfast. The price you pay for a double sausage and egg McMuffin, one supposes.

Industry observers note that the sound quality is a highlight of the Noise Canceling Wired Earbuds. The bass is less in your face than prior models, although it’s a lovely addition to the table. Similarly, high-range and lower-register mids sound great no matter the genre you’re listening to. It's a less in-your-face audio experience than previous Bose products, which is a nice change.

Then there’s the wire, which comes with both pros and cons. You don’t have to worry about battery life, for one. The power for the ANC is pulled straight from your phone or laptops battery, so your earbuds will only die when your listening device does. That’s good. You also get lossless audio thanks to the USB-C connection, and low-latency listening should you want to play games or watch movies and TV shows on the go without the sound getting behind what’s going on on-screen.

The bad thing? You’re tethered. Forget to unplug them or take them out when you stand up and you’ll send your phone flying across the floor or violently disconnect them from your laptop. You’ll need to get used to it, that’s for sure. But for under $100? It’s well worth the trade-off, if not only for effectively unlimited battery life.

It has been revealed that we test a lot of noise-canceling earbuds, but not everything can make it into our buying guides. Whether that's down to better performance or stronger features from rival models in a particular category and price, some miss ranking in this list by the slightest of margins. With that in mind, these models are strong contenders and great alternative considerations.

Industry observers note that apple's new noise-canceling earbuds are here, and they land at a lower price than the previous model. We were impressed with the ANC this time around, although the battery life simply isn't good enough to kick it with the options above. Still, Apple consumers on a budget will find a lot to like here.

The ZE300 are Final’s lightest earbuds yet, and they’re perhaps some of the most comfortable buds out there right now. For less than $50, you’re getting excellent sound quality across many genres and highly effective ANC indoors, packaged into a pressure-relieving design with a comfortable fit.

Read our full Final ZE300 review.

A strong pair of cheap wireless noise-canceling earbuds, the EarFun Pro 3 deliver nearly 40 hours of listening (with their case), making them some of the longest-lasting among their peers like the Soundcore Liberty 4 NC. The ANC in the EarFun set is effective and the buds also support aptX Adaptive audio, and have a custom equalizer in its app. Our review also mentioned the good call quality and wireless charging.

Read our full EarFun Air Pro 3 review.

Soundcore has finally joined the major leagues, although the Liberty 5 Pro Max aren't quite up there with the best yet. They sound good and offer some useful features, but we'd say you're still better off with the buds from Sony, Apple and Bose right now.

Read our full Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max review.

We've judged the best noise-canceling earbuds on several factors: audio performance, battery life, Bluetooth range, call quality, comfort and fit, and the effectiveness of the noise cancellation. We also weigh special features, such as included apps, and how easy they are to use.

During the testing phase, our reviewers wear each pair of earbuds for 2 hours at a time throughout the course of a week, to test comfort over time.

ANC, meanwhile, is tested in both indoor and outdoor environments where ambient sounds are produced at high levels. This includes airplanes, city parks, convenience shops, offices, and public transportation. ANC earbuds programmed with transparency modes are also tested thoroughly to determine how well the listener can hear their surroundings.

In a recent development, for sound quality, we listen to many different sample tracks and span as many music genres as possible, including hip-hop, rock, jazz, classical and R&B, while evaluating volume, clarity, and fullness. Find out what we listen for during our testing process and how to get the best headphone sound for you.

And now that more streaming music services are offering high-resolution audio, be sure to read our audio codec FAQ for all you need to know.

According to recent reports, finally, we’ll rate noise-canceling earbuds on our five-point system, with 1 being the worst and 5 the best. If a pair is particularly excellent, with a robust range of qualities, we may award it an Editor's Choice badge.

Recent findings suggest that the first item to check off the list when shopping for the best noise-canceling earbuds is their active noise cancellation performance, which shouldn’t be confused with passive noise cancellation. What are the differences?

According to recent reports, 1. Active vs. passive noise cancellation: ANC uses advanced circuitry and microphones to pick up noise signals and create inverse waves that cancel out these sonic disruptions, whereas PNC physically isolates high-pitched sounds through the headphone design and materials. Most headphones advertised with noise cancellation are categorized under ANC.

2. Battery life: Noise-canceling earbuds have a reputation for sucking up lots of power, so you’ll want a pair that holds a charge long enough to get you through a long business flight or weekly commutes. Noise-canceling wireless earbuds are usually rated for 4.5 to 8 hours, but with included charging cases the total possible playback time might be much more competitive.

It has been revealed that think about how long and how often you’d want to wear your earbuds for on lengthy trips. A longer “per charge” battery life is better, but if you only want some entertainment on short commutes then it not quite so crucial, as you’ll probably be storing the buds in their case more regularly.

Recent findings suggest that 3. Sound quality: ANC technology can compress sound and reduce dynamics, which may affect audio performance when turned on. In some cases, you’ll notice a background hiss when listening to music. However, the best noise-canceling earbuds limit these disruptions to deliver full, crisp sound.

It has been revealed that 4. Design: The look, build and feel of a pair of in-ear 'buds is massively crucial when selecting the best noise-canceling earbuds, so consider how they look and feel and whether the style is right for you. In our best noise-canceling headphones round up we mention that over-ear headphones tend to give the best noise cancellation, but some of the more recent wireless in-ear models are proving to be just as effective.

According to recent reports, 5. Pricing considerations: Obviously, price is a massive consideration when looking for the best noise-canceling earbuds. Although there are always exceptions, big-name brands will typically command a bit extra, but generally speaking, the less you spend on a pair of headphones the greater the chance that sound and features will be compromised. Going for a budget option isn't always the best choice, as any money you save on your purchase won't do you much good if you're constantly needing to recharge your audio gear, or the sound quality is poor.

ANC explained: Active noise cancellation (ANC) models employ built-in mics to pick up ambient sounds around the wearer. An identical but inverted audio signal of the noise is played back to the listener through the headphones.

According to recent reports, listeners aren't aware of this happening of course, as the inverted (or out of phase) signal effectively 'cancels out' the noise of the surroundings for the headphone wearer. The process removes the external sounds, which results in a significant reduction in the level of background noise at the very least.

Given that it uses both more computational power and a bunch of microphones in order to work, ANC has an effect on your battery life. This often chops a couple of hours off, so they won't last quite as long. If you want to keep the battery going for longer then you'll want to keep the noise canceling turned off.

In most cases, noise-canceling earbuds are very effective at reducing ambient sounds. There are limits, though, and some designs are less effective at silencing certain types of sounds than others.

The process is fast but it can’t physically occur in real time, so active noise cancellation (ANC) works best with consistent low-frequency sounds as opposed to higher-pitched, inconsistent sounds like human speech.

Vehicle engines and droning air conditioners are easy to cancel out, but the shorter wavelength of high-frequency sounds, like a sudden blast from a car horn, makes it tougher for the ANC’s anti-noise waves to perfectly mask these bursts.

Even so, all sounds will be at least a little quieter when you’re wearing noise-canceling headphones, and many sounds can be completely silenced even on low-cost pairs or earbuds.

Here in the World: Letters of Albert Camus, 1944–1959

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1316 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that what an amazing behemoth of a book!
  • Sources indicate that on D-Day, Camus was thirty; Casarès was twenty-one.
  • The correspondence was first published in French in 2017; now it has been (brilliantly) translated by Sandra Smith and Cory Stockwell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that what an amazing behemoth of a book! I’ve been lugging it around for weeks. Nearly a thousand letters: the intimate correspondence of Albert Camus and Maria Casarès. When they first met in Paris – on D-Day, 1944 – Camus had already published L’Etranger (1942; The Outsider). Born and raised in Algeria, he was in Paris when the Second World War broke out, and later joined the French Resistance. Camus’s wife, Francine Faure, a mathematician and pianist, remained in Algeria. Maria Casarès was originally from Galicia, the daughter of an exiled former prime minister of Spain, Santiago Casares Quiroga. In 1944, Casarès was already known as an actress, having played the titular role in J M Synge’s Deirdre of the Sorrows. She later starred in Les Enfants du paradis (1945), Cocteau’s Orphée (1950) and La Lectrice (1988), among other films and plays.

Sources indicate that on D-Day, Camus was thirty; Casarès was twenty-one. They began an affair, but this ended when Camus was reunited with his wife. In 1945, Faure gave birth to twins: Catherine and Jean. In June 1948, Camus and Casarès met again and embarked on a long relationship, which continued until Camus’s death in a car crash on 4 January 1960. Afterwards, the poet René Char found Casarès’s letters in Camus’s apartment and discreetly returned them to her. In the 1990s, not long before she died, Casarès offered the letters to Camus’s daughter, Catherine.

The correspondence was first published in French in 2017; now it has been (brilliantly) translated by Sandra Smith and Cory Stockwell. The letters are passionate, voluminous, at times torrential. Everything is discussed: love, sex, books, plays, films, beauty, art, family, madness, fear of failure, fear of death. Also logistics, travel looks, inadequate postal services, money troubles, indigestion, hives, headaches.

Industry observers note that in her preface, Catherine Camus writes: ‘Their letters make the earth more vast, space more luminous, the air lighter, simply because they existed.’ Casarès, she believes, is ‘like the ocean: breaking, crashing, re-forming and starting over again with stupefying vitality’. Camus is pretty oceanic as well. Both lovers travelled extensively; the letters are often scrawled in haste, sent from Paris, Cabris, Oran, from North and South America, written on ocean liners, or ended abruptly to catch the post. Sometimes, too, they are written as a sort of diary, across several days. The tempo changes. There are lists, schedules; they want to know what the other has been doing, hour by hour. How many glasses of wine they’ve drunk. What they’ve eaten. Who they’ve seen. There are ecstatic protestations of love. And questions, lots of questions. What happened last night? Are you happy? Did you see a doctor? They both emerge vividly – fascinating, erudite, witty, anxious; flawed and paradoxical.

As Catherine Camus notes, there is great luminosity; many descriptions of humid summer nights, bright oceans, shimmering mountains. Also, a rich sense of being finite and alive, briefly here in the world: ‘I didn’t sleep any better last night, and tonight it’s so hot, there are so many crickets and stars that I have no hope of falling asleep. At least I can write to you…’ (Camus). Or, ‘Today the sky, which was a drab deep gray this morning, gradually brightened up, and around 2:00, you could just about see the sun peeking through a soft veil’ (Casarès). They struggle with grief, sorrow and anxiety, with physical asperities. Camus endures savage bouts of TB, ‘getting undressed again, letting myself be poked and prodded’. For a while, Francine Faure is depressed, consigned to a hospital, repeating the name ‘Maria Casarès’. Camus and Casarès agonise about her. Sometimes, they argue furiously: ‘You’re stupid, my poor darling!’ writes Casarès, ‘and we must wait for it to pass!’ The war has ended, cities lie in ruins, everything feels untethered and surreal: ‘Of course, the world is still sick, even if I’m well,’ writes Camus. ‘Will we always have to love each other during the Apocalypse, in anguish, in torment?’.

It has been revealed that often, they discuss books and authors. They’re not fans of Hemingway. On reading To Have and Have Not (1937), Casarès writes: ‘I certainly found some well-written pages but, my God, how dusty, dull, gloomy it all is, and it smells so much of rooms with peeling wall­paper, all of them a mess, with the odor of sheets, night sweats and dirty clothes!’ Camus’s response is yet more scathing: ‘Hemingway? It serves you right! Why read phonies with no talent?’ Proust gets a mixed review: Casarès is ‘hooked’, loves the way he writes about nature, but finds the ‘political gossip’ boring. In January 1950, Camus sends ‘bad news’:.

George Orwell died. You don’t know him. A very talented English writer, who had the same experience as me, more or less (even though he’s ten years older), and exactly the same ideas. He’d been fighting tuberculosis for years. He was one of a very small number of men with whom I shared something.

Both Camus and Orwell opposed the adamantine absolutes of communism and fascism; both were attacked for their political views. They had arranged to see each other in Paris in 1945, but Camus was afflicted by another bout of TB and the meeting never happened. A few months after Orwell’s death, Camus gives a copy of Nineteen Eighty-Four to Casarès. She isn’t convinced: ‘I didn’t learn anything from it that I hadn’t already imagined, and it left a weak impression on me.’.

When it comes to his own books, Camus is full of self-doubt, grappling with his ‘tormented, mistrustful soul’. He works ‘like a madman’ on L’Homme revolté (1951; The Rebel), but fears it is a failure: ‘I only hope that this book won’t be too far from what it was meant to be. I hope it will help people to live – that it will say that all is not lost – that it will give everyone with whom I feel solidarity the strength to hate nothing, and to create.’ Even after receiving the Nobel Prize in 1957, Camus is still ‘trying to find some equilibrium within myself’. As for Casarès, in one of the last letters she describes herself as ‘here, a little shapeless, it’s true – a little like you, perhaps, or like the world that surrounds us – but I’m here nonetheless, whole and alive’. It’s impossible to know if they wrote with any sense of eventual publication in mind, or simply and entirely for each other. Camus usually drafted and redrafted his published works. Even his Notebooks were edited – by Camus himself, and by Francine Faure, among others. In the end, these letters are so surreally intimate, so poetic and unbridled, that it feels a bit like reading an extraordinary epistolary novel: about love, art, war, finitude and crazy-­beautiful optimism. All is not lost indeed.

With the upcoming system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

In a recent development, as I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The new sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

The Apple Watch lineup is incredibly strong right now. Whether you’re deciding between the SE 3 and Series 12, both offer great health tracking, battery life, and connectivity. The Apple Watch SE 3 is an excellent choice for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem.

The Apple Watch Series 12, however, is the best Apple Watch for most people. There are major improvements to the health tracking capabilities, offering meaningful steps forward in what the Apple Watch can tell you about yourself. In the two months I’ve had mine, I’ve come to appreciate the more frequent heart rate measurement and readiness score.

Offering support for iPhone and Android’s tracking networks, the upcoming Kodak SlideTag offers the neat added functionality over an AirTag of being able to show your photos and more on an E-Ink display.

The Kodak SlideTag is inspired by classic 35mm slides from Kodak cameras, and is built by the same firm, Reto, that debuted a keychain digital camera inspired by old Kodak cameras too. The tracker’s E-Ink display is designed mainly to showcase your photos, with storage built-in for up to 12 photos, but also the ability to show lists and QR codes.

The SlideTag’s extra features are controlled by the Kodak Memory Link app, while tracking is handled in the Find My app on iPhone just like an AirTag (and the Find Hub app on Android phones).

Recent findings suggest that there are nine total styles for the SlideTag, all sold in a blind box format. You can order one tracker for $35 with the whole set also available for purchase.

Eight of the styles have a one-in-eight chance of finding, while the ninth style is only found in one out of every 64 boxes.

Kodak SlideTag is available today from Amazon.

Breaking: I’ve been testing the Coros Vertix 4 for 5 days — here’s what I like and dislike about the Garmin Fenix rival so far

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1495 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coros has launched the Vertix 4 as its new flagship smartwatch, and it’s a major upgrade over the Coros Vertix 2S with an AMOLED display, a more attractive design that has a built-in flashlight, and satellite maps.
  • I’ve been testing the Vertix 4 for five days, which isn’t nearly enough time to get through its extensive battery life, but I have been able to get some first impressions of the watch by doing four runs with it, comparing it directly to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro.
  • It has been revealed that you’ll find my early likes and dislikes for the Coros Vertix 4 below, along with its price and specs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coros has launched the Vertix 4 as its new flagship smartwatch, and it’s a major upgrade over the Coros Vertix 2S with an AMOLED display, a more attractive design that has a built-in flashlight, and satellite maps.

I’ve been testing the Vertix 4 for five days, which isn’t nearly enough time to get through its extensive battery life, but I have been able to get some first impressions of the watch by doing four runs with it, comparing it directly to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro.

It has been revealed that you’ll find my early likes and dislikes for the Coros Vertix 4 below, along with its price and specs. For those wondering why Coros went from 2S to 4, skipping a Vertix 3, it’s to bring the Vertix 4 into line with its other watches: the Coros Apex 4 and Coros Pace 4 Pro.

According to recent reports, the Coros Vertix 4 debuted on 24 November 2026 and will be available to order from 27 November. It costs $799 in the U.S. and £669 in the U.K., a $100/£70 price rise on the Vertix 2S.

It does come in significantly cheaper than the latest Garmin Fenix 9 line-up, though, which starts at $999. However, there are some rivals that come in cheaper than the Vertix 4, with the Suunto Vertical 2 titanium model, costing $699/£639, and older Garmin Fenix models appearing in sales — the Garmin Fenix 8 is $749 at Amazon right now, for example.

The Vertix has previously had a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display, and while that does have some advantages, most notably longer battery life, I much prefer the AMOLED display on the Vertix 4.

It’s a very major, bright screen and easier to read than the MIP display on the Vertix 2S in all conditions I find, even in bright sunlight.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The upcoming satellite maps also look great on the display, and the battery life on the Vertix 4 is still very good.

While it would have been great for Coros to make the Vertix 4 available with both MIP and AMOLED options, as Garmin does with the Fenix, it’s perhaps not practical in production terms, and I do think AMOLED is the better option here, with the Apex 4 offering a MIP alternative in the Coros line-up.

Adventure watches are, by design, significant and bold devices to strap to your wrist, but the Vertix 2S was a little too huge, and the Coros Vertix 4 is a much more enjoyable watch to wear all day.

It’s thinner and lighter than its predecessor while having a larger display, and doesn’t feel too bulky even on my slim wrist.

In the past, I think Coros watches could be accused of prioritizing substance over style, which is no bad thing, but it’s better to have both, and both of the brand’s 2026 introduces — the Pace 4 Pro and now Vertix 4 — have been more attractive than past options.

Ever since Garmin added a built-in flashlight to the Fenix 7X, it’s been a feature that people have wanted in their smartwatch, and the Vertix 4 is the first Coros watch to get it.

Coros has swerved from the usual flashlight setup used by other brands, though, sticking its light on the side of the Vertix 4, between the digital dial and back button, as opposed to on the top as Garmin, Suunto and Amazfit do.

This has its advantages — the flashlight naturally focuses the way your arm is pointing, and you can switch the orientation of the buttons on the watch if you wear it on your right wrist.

I’m still on the fence about whether I prefer this or having the flashlight on top of the watch, but ultimately it’s a major addition to the Vertix line in general, and a very handy feature to have.

Another interesting upcoming feature on the Vertix 4 is satellite maps, which you can download to the watch and use instead of the standard maps. This is a feature I’m testing in beta, with it expected to launch in early 2027.

The satellite maps look great on the AMOLED display, and at times, it's a bit clearer to see what’s around you using them, especially in the forest.

It was pretty quick and easy to get my local area onto the watch through the Coros app, though the satellite map files are larger than the standard, so you will want to be choosy with the areas you download to the watch.

While the standard maps on the watch work fine, having the satellite option is useful at times, and it differentiates the Vertix 4 from other brands since these maps are free.

The Vertix 2S offers incredible battery life — it lasted me 22 days on a charge and even outperformed the Garmin Enduro 2 on this front.

Given the switch to an AMOLED display, the fear would be that the Vertix 4 fell short on this front in comparison, but the listed stats are still very impressive for the watch.

Coros suggests it will last up to 30 days in watch mode, or 10 days with the screen always on, and it offers 48 hours of multi-band GPS tracking with the screen always on.

So far, the Vertix is on track to beat those estimates for me, although aided by the fact that I haven't used it for sleep tracking so far.

With the screen always on and running every day using the most accurate multi-band mode, it’s on track to last over 10 days.

All the Coros watches launched over the past couple of years have impressed me with their GPS accuracy, and that’s the case with the Vertix 4 so far as well.

In a recent development, I’ve been running with it and the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro, with both set to their most accurate mode, and checking the GPS tracks afterwards. The Vertix 4 tracks have been spot on and in line with the Fenix 9 Pro on pace and distance stats throughout the runs too.

Unlike GPS accuracy, the heart rate accuracy of the Vertix 4 has been a bit iffy in my early testing when comparing the readings to a chest strap.

In the Vertix 4’s defence, I’ve been testing it in cold weather, when optical sensors on watches do tend to be less accurate, but I’ve still been a little underwhelmed by the results.

On my easy runs, it’s mostly been pretty close to a chest strap, but on a hard progression run, the Vertix 4’s readings were too high throughout. Based on my early tests, you’d definitely be wise to pair a chest strap to the Vertix 4, at least in cold conditions.

The Vertix 4 is noticeably slimmer and lighter than past versions, but it’s still quite a big watch, and Coros does not offer any size options, something that Garmin does with the Fenix 9.

There are the Apex 4 and Pace 4 Pro as smaller alternatives in the Coros line-up, but if you want the flagship model, you have to accept that it only comes in one size, and it’s a biggie.

It doesn’t take long when testing a Coros watch to realize that they really make sports watches, not smartwatches.

Sources indicate that the Vertix 4 can store music, but only files you drag and drop onto the watch; it doesn’t pair with streaming services. It also doesn’t offer NFC payments, and you can’t customize the watch face as much as on rivals.

Personally, I don’t miss these smart features much, but they are a selling point not only true smartwatches like the Apple Watch Ultra 4, but also Garmin watches, which combine great sports tracking with useful smarts.

#188417. Can an App Tell When Someone Near You Is Wearing Smart Glasses?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1274 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

Can an App Tell When Someone Near You Is Wearing Smart Glasses?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1274 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that meta’s smart glasses stay connected to the wearer’s phone over Bluetooth, and that connection is what detector apps look for.
  • It’s a clever workaround for glasses designed to blend in.
  • Here’s how those apps work, what they reliably catch and what they miss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that meta’s smart glasses stay connected to the wearer’s phone over Bluetooth, and that connection is what detector apps look for. Apps such as Zuckoff scan for the short broadcast signals Bluetooth devices send out and compare them with signals from known smart glasses models. When there’s a match, the app sends an alert. It’s a practical way to learn that a pair is nearby, though the alert can’t confirm whether anyone’s recording, and glasses with Bluetooth switched off won’t appear at all. Here’s how the apps work and how much weight to give an alert.

It’s a clever workaround for glasses designed to blend in. How useful it is depends on what you want it to tell you: The app can detect that a pair is close by, but not whether it’s recording. Still, that’s more notice than most people get today, especially if they haven’t spotted the glasses’ built-in LED indicator.

Here’s how those apps work, what they reliably catch and what they miss.

Sources indicate that broad concerns over privacy have led to a technical battle. On one side, hardware modifiers are tweaking wearable cameras to make them even harder to spot, often by disabling LED indicators. On the other, developers and privacy-focused coders are launching counter tech to give you a heads-up when a hidden camera walks into the room.

Zuckoff, whose name takes a direct jab at Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, has joined a small ecosystem of apps such as Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner and Nearby Glasses that offer similar functionality — letting you know when someone has smart glasses activated and how close the device is, although they can’t tell you specifically whether someone is actively recording or using AI to pull up information. The apps detect approximate device proximity by sweeping local Bluetooth frequencies to locate vendor IDs, system identifiers and hardware signatures associated with smart glasses.

According to recent reports, as Zuckoff’s website notes: “Glasses advertise loudest while powering on, pairing or leaving the case. Once paired to their owner’s phone, they can go quiet, so silence is not proof that nobody is recording, and a detection is not proof that anyone is. Signal strength gives a rough distance and no direction at all.”.

Zuckoff’s developer, Pawel Szydlowski, remarked he was already working on projects that used Bluetooth to detect nearby devices and discovered the tech could be applied to smart glasses. “It’s just the same technology wrapped in a different paper,” he said in a video chat with CNET.

Recent reports have shown that smart glasses are being used for everything from bullying in schools to viral videos with unwitting subjects who don’t know they’re being recorded.

What drove Szydlowski to actively develop a software detector was seeing social media videos of people wearing smart glasses who recorded pranks or harassed women with pickup lines. None of the targets seemed aware that their content would appear online, which made Szydlowski angry. “There was not even a blur involved to try to censor them, to give them some sort of feeling of privacy,” he noted. “These days, everybody feels entitled to post everything.”.

Recent findings suggest that since it launched in early August, the Zuckoff app has gotten 2,000 sign-ups, and Szydlowski is beta-testing an Android version he hopes to make available on the Google Play Store. The app also has a premium version for $10 a year that can run continuous detection checks in the background when the app isn’t in use.

But a booming ecosystem of DIY modifications and third-party hardware hacks is also giving smart glasses wearers unprecedented stealth by allowing them to disable the activation lights, either by bypassing the capture LEDs or by patching software to suppress system notifications.

Tech journalist Joanna Stern hosted a video showing the process in which a local hacker removed the LED light from her Ray-Ban Meta glasses for $100, allowing the wearables to secretly record without notice.

It has been revealed that detecting active smart glasses in public or private spaces adds a upcoming layer of security awareness, but it raises an obvious dilemma: What do you actually do with that information? Once a detector app alerts us that smart glasses are nearby, it seems our only choices are to either leave the space or ask the wearer to remove the glasses.

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an associate professor of information systems at the University of Washington who studies the societal impacts of technology, notes we’re still figuring out the social norms around wearables like smart glasses. It’s impossible to know whether the person filming will behave responsibly, and the question of consent gets even thornier if children might be captured on video or in photos.

Unlike with smartphones, where it’s easier to tell when someone is recording or taking photos, “smart glasses shift the burden of privacy entirely onto the person being photographed,” Ananthakrishnan mentioned.

“Until we develop clear mechanisms to balance seamless innovation with consent, these devices will continue to turn everyday public spaces into zones of surveillance anxiety,” she stated.

That surveillance anxiety may prompt some hardware makers to release alternative versions of smart glasses that entirely avoid potential privacy violations.

According to recent reports, the Even G2 smart glasses don’t have a camera for recording photos or videos. They can pair with a separately sold R1 control ring that works as a fitness tracker.

For instance, Even Realities’ G2 smart glasses don’t include a front-facing camera at all. Instead, the Even G2 devices, released in late 2025, focus on providing the wearer with information and acting more like a personal assistant.

“We made the decision from the beginning that smart glasses don’t need to have cameras on them in order to be useful,” Even Realities CEO Will Wang told CNET in an email. “We believe something worn on your face should respect not only the person wearing it, but everyone around them.”.

The G2 devices don’t record externally, a design choice Wang remarked gave the manufacturer a unique challenge. “Leaving the camera out also pushed us to think differently about what actually makes smart glasses useful day to day, rather than assuming more sensors automatically make a better product,” he said.

According to recent reports, wang remarked there’s room in the smart glasses market for different approaches to features and functionality, and that buyers may want to make trade-offs for devices they’ll wear on their faces. But Wang noted that the rise of smart glasses detectors indicates that social acceptance is an concern the industry needs to consider.

Over the last several months, smart glasses have been getting cheaper. And with more models and companies jumping into the fray, the demand for surveillance detectors is likely to grow — that is, unless Big Tech and wearable companies radically change their devices to make them invisible to detector apps.

Zuckoff’s Szydlowski mentioned it’s possible a organization could shrink the kind of 5G technology to fit in smart glasses, making them less dependent on phones and Bluetooth, but that’s unlikely to happen anytime soon. If Meta or Snap deliberately updated their hardware to hide from detection apps and disable smart glasses’ digital footprint, it would further undercut any claim of privacy accountability.

Szydlowski mentioned his hope is that, in time, Zuckoff won’t be needed at all. He pointed out that the ability to detect nearby Apple AirTag devices eventually became part of the operating systems on iOS and Android devices. If consumers pressure manufacturers and their governments to make smart glasses easier to detect, it would be “the perfect solution” to make his app obsolete, he said.

Signal to restrict screenshots over AI agent concerns – again

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Privacy concerns around AI agents have prompted encrypted messaging app Signal to set upcoming limits on screenshots.
  • It has been revealed that whittaker noted that Google and Apple’s agentic features, including Gemini Intelligence and Siri AI’s Onscreen Awareness, compromise the privacy missions of third-party developers.
  • Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks – and why.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Privacy concerns around AI agents have prompted encrypted messaging app Signal to set upcoming limits on screenshots. The company will prevent screenshotting in its iOS 27 app and “when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android,” Signal President Meredith Whittaker wrote in a blog post Friday.

It has been revealed that whittaker noted that Google and Apple’s agentic features, including Gemini Intelligence and Siri AI’s Onscreen Awareness, compromise the privacy missions of third-party developers. These features observe what’s on a user’s screen as context for completing requests.

Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks – and why.

In a recent development, “Your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” Whittaker mentioned. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”.

Signal also blocked screenshots last year in response to Microsoft’s controversial Recall AI feature, which could capture screenshots of Signal chats on devices running Windows 11.

Signal’s move is another reminder of how Substantial Tech’s AI strategy trickles downstream. As AI features have moved from services external to the OS (like chatbots from OpenAI or Anthropic) to further inside of it, third-party apps have to adapt to conditions that undermine their hard-won privacy infrastructure.

Also: How I use Meta Muse safely to stretch my AI budget – and what I never let it do.

Recent findings suggest that just last week, researchers at Google DeepMind used AI agents to formally verify Signal’s code, building on Signal’s own work to essentially prove the app’s encryption works. That’s a high bar for a security guarantee within the app, but it becomes meaningless if an agent can simply grab messages off a screen.

Samsung is reportedly working on its own agent, Galaxy Claw, and Apple is developing a rival for Claude and ChatGPT as well.

Whittaker noted Signal’s screenshot restriction isn’t perfect, saying that AI agents can still access app data through other means, “such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.” Earlier this week, a Reuters investigation supported by Signal and the AI Now Institute found that Meta’s Muse AI agent was using permissions from its initial setup in unexpected ways to access apps and data that a user had not explicitly connected it to.

Signal stated its protections don’t presently work on MacOS.

“It is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” she added. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience.”.

If you’d still like to take screenshots, you can simply disable the setting, though Signal’s announcement strongly advised against it.

“Doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees,” Whittaker remarked.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

Jetty Pro

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that my first two Mac apps, Front and Center and SwitchGlass, were both created back in 2020 to restore features from DragThing, the venerable Mac app that was retired in 2019.
  • After 24 years of development, DragThing had a ton of features.
  • Perhaps to prove them wrong, the next app I created was Hyperspace, which provided a way to reclaim disk space without removing any files.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that my first two Mac apps, Front and Center and SwitchGlass, were both created back in 2020 to restore features from DragThing, the venerable Mac app that was retired in 2019. The one tiny feature that Front and Center provided was literally a single checkbox within DragThing’s preferences. SwitchGlass went a bit farther, recreating one specific kind of floating palette from DragThing (and classic Mac OS).

After 24 years of development, DragThing had a ton of features. People often joked that I was destined to slowly reimplement all of DragThing’s functionality in a series of small apps. Put another way, they were saying I was doomed to make strange little Mac apps with extremely limited appeal (and sales).

Perhaps to prove them wrong, the next app I created was Hyperspace, which provided a way to reclaim disk space without removing any files. Hyperspace was still a nerdy app, but at least it had somewhat broader appeal than my earlier efforts. Who doesn’t want to save disk space? But more importantly, it was totally unrelated to DragThing. I had broken the curse!

According to recent reports, alas, there was one more (small) thing from DragThing that I missed. I used to have a DragThing palette in the corner of my screen containing some commonly used folders. In earlier versions of macOS, it was possible to pin the Dock to a screen corner, but that wasn’t really what I wanted either. I just wanted a small, separate palette of folders in the corner.

According to recent reports, this is not a hard problem to solve. Plenty of Mac apps can provide something close to what I want…but not exactly what I want, in the specific way that I want it. For many years, I got by with some folders in the corner of my desktop. But the problem nagged at me.

In a recent development, A few years ago, I went so far as to implement my desired feature in SwitchGlass, adding the ability to create a small, extra palette full of folders in addition to the app switcher. But it felt incongruous with the rest of the app, so I never shipped it. And I didn’t want to maintain my own private fork of SwitchGlass, so I abandoned that branch of the code.

It has been revealed that today, AI coding agents are helping to produce a bounty of fresh, niche Mac apps, many made by people who have little or no coding experience. Even for experienced software developers, vibe coding has made it possible to create apps that were previously “not worth building” due to an unfavorable ratio of effort to payoff.

It’s in this context that I revisited my “little palette of folders” idea. Surely I could vibe-code a simple app just for me in a day or two, right?

That was three and a half months ago.

Industry observers note that so what happened? The well-known programmer’s credo comes to mind: “We do these things not because they are easy, but because we thought they would be easy.” Indeed.

Sources indicate that I began the project by feeding a coding agent the source code to my app, SwitchGlass, as a starting point. I wrote SwitchGlass six years ago using a substantially more primitive version of SwiftUI. (For the developers out there, it predates @Observable and @State, and it supports Macs all the way back to macOS 12 Monterey from 2021.) I asked a coding agent to modernize the code and generalize it to support an arbitrary number of palettes instead of just one app switcher palette per display.

Industry observers note that it worked, and quickly! But it was pretty shoddy. Many optimizations and niceties from SwitchGlass had been lost. So I dove in to fix them…and maybe add one or two more features, I guess….

Industry observers note that now, after months of work, I’ve created a bit of a monster. But in the process, I’ve fulfilled a long-held dream of mine—a dream I had set aside years ago because I thought it was impossible. I’ve replaced the Dock.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve read any of my Mac OS X reviews, you know that I’ve always been dissatisfied with the Dock. Over the past couple of decades, I’ve gotten used to it, but I still bump up against its limitations and undesirable behaviors every day. (Undesirable to me, anyway.).

To pick just one example, I’ve always wanted clicking on a folder in the Dock to open that folder in the Finder. The Dock did work this way for several years, but in 2009’s Mac OS X 10.6 Snow Leopard (…I think?), Apple switched to requiring a Command-Option-click to open a folder in the Finder. Since then, I’ve been Command-Option-clicking folders in the Dock many, many times per day. It’s a small thing, but it adds up: seventeen years of Command-Option clicking!

Sources indicate that but what could I do? I was forced to continue to use the Dock because there are so many things that “only the Dock can do” in macOS. I was reminded of this harsh reality when I created SwitchGlass. Why doesn’t SwitchGlass show notification badges? Why does the Calendar icon show today’s date in the Dock but not in SwitchGlass? Why don’t app icons in SwitchGlass bounce when the app needs attention? Why can’t I quit an app from SwitchGlass?

Though I did find a workaround for that last one, the answer to most of these questions is that third-party apps simply can’t do all the things the Dock can do. The Dock is part of the operating system, and it enjoys special privileges and deep integration that no third-party app can match.

This remains true today, especially for sandboxed apps sold through the Mac App Store like SwitchGlass (and all my other Mac apps). But what about apps that aren’t in the Mac App Store? What about unsandboxed apps? How close can they come to doing all the things the Dock does, especially if they use private APIs that are forbidden in the Mac App Store?

In a recent development, I aimed to find out. I hatched a proposal, which I unveiled on episode 706 of Accidental Tech Podcast on August 26, 2026. I would create two apps: one called Jetty that would be sold through the Mac App Store, and a more powerful, unsandboxed app called Jetty Pro that would be distributed directly to customers, outside the Mac App Store.

Sources indicate that but as I worked on the two apps, it became clear that “plain Jetty” was not that great. It had all the same limitations as SwitchGlass when it came to duplicating the features of the Dock. After less than two weeks of work, I abandoned plain Jetty and concentrated entirely on Jetty Pro.

After three and a half months of work, there are still things that only the Dock can do, but the list is not very long. I don’t expect most users to fully replace the Dock with Jetty Pro, but I’m happily doing so. If only my 2001 self could see me now!

Industry observers note that now, finally, I’d like to introduce Jetty Pro: an app that creates customizable Dock-like floating palettes around the edges of your Mac’s displays. These palettes can contain any combination of files, folders, volumes, apps, Shortcuts, spacers, dividers, and even the Trash. If you’ve ever been unsatisfied with some aspect of how the the Dock works, or if you’ve just wanted to augment the Dock with some additional palettes, try Jetty Pro and make your Mac’s interface work the way you want it to. Here are some of the highlights:.

Industry observers note that jetty Pro palettes are extensively customizable. Nearly every palette layout metric can be adjusted. Jetty Pro can simulate the Dock backgrounds from macOS 15, 26, and 27, and it provides several of its own background appearances as well. The image at the top of this post indicates just some of the possibilities.

Jetty Pro lets you customize the icon of any item in a palette—even the Finder. And if you’ve ever wanted to break an app out of Squircle Jail, now you can do it.

Unlike the macOS Dock, Jetty Pro will show folder label colors (without also setting a folder symbol). You can even apply color labels to folders independent of their labels in the Finder.

According to recent reports, don’t want to see “Running in Background” apps in macOS 27? Jetty Pro can hide them.

Want to hide notification badges for specific apps, but only in specific palettes? Jetty Pro can do that. And unlike the Dock, Jetty Pro can even hide notification badges on the System Settings app.

Jetty Pro can exclude or include running apps of your choice on a per-palette basis.

Jetty Pro lets you choose what happens when you click (or modifier-click) an app or folder in a palette.

A Jetty Pro palette can be configured to appear on a single display, selected displays, or on every display, while also choosing which attributes, like size and position, are allowed to vary per display.

Use Jetty Pro to augment the macOS Dock with additional palettes, or use it to replace the Dock entirely. It’s up to you.

Jetty Pro is available for a special introductory price of $9.99 per year (plus applicable taxes) until the end of 2026, with a 14-day free trial.

Download Jetty Pro 14-day Free Trial.

To learn more, including why a subscription is the only way to pay for Jetty Pro, please read the extensive documentation.

Sources indicate that as you might have already guessed, Jetty Pro uses every private API it can get its hands on, and it requires a ton of special permissions, all of which are explained in the documentation. For sensible security reasons, macOS makes it (increasingly) cumbersome for people to grant these permissions. But Jetty Pro needs them to do what it does. Check Settings > General in Jetty Pro and make sure it states “All permissions have been granted” at the bottom. If not, click the “Details…” button for further instructions.

After a brief dalliance with more “mainstream” apps like Hyperspace, I’m back to making niche apps for Mac weirdos like me. To thine own self be true, I guess. I hope there are others out there who have longed to make the Dock work just slightly differently and are now able to do so thanks to Jetty Pro.

I’m sure many people reading this will think it’s ridiculous that I spent months battling the limitations of macOS to create what appears (to the undiscerning eye) to be a nearly identical clone of the Dock. What a waste of time! And what took so long anyway? This is a weekend project, at most!

First, I can assure you that the “simple” appearance of Jetty Pro belies the huge level of complexity and trickery required to do so many different things that macOS does not support and actively works against. If Jetty Pro really does seem simple in use, then I have done my job well. (And if you can see the seams, then that’s where I’ve failed to completely overcome a hostile system that doesn’t want to allow Jetty Pro to do what it needs to do.).

According to recent reports, second, I put a tremendous amount of time and effort into Jetty Pro. The documentation alone (which, like every word in every post on this website, was written by me and me alone) took weeks to create. During the lead up to Jetty Pro 1.0, I’ve released over 160 builds to my 250 beta testers—more than one build per day. The Jetty Pro app icon was created by the fine humans at The Iconfactory. From the start, I’ve treated Jetty Pro like a “real” app, not a throwaway vibe-coded project.

Sources indicate that having spent so many years with the Dock as a tiny pebble in my shoe, the difference between it and Jetty Pro means everything to me. Like Front and Center and SwitchGlass before it, I’m now running Jetty Pro all day, every day on my Mac. Replacing the Dock with Jetty Pro has made me happier than any other app I’ve created. I hope it will make some other Mac weirdos happy too.

Heart attack and stroke risk detectable decades in advance

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Early warning signs could help doctors predict those at risk of a heart attack or stroke up to 30 years before an event, research suggests.
  • Scientists identified early patterns in a range of risk factors for cardiovascular disease – conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels – including high blood pressure, diabetes and kidney function.
  • They also revealed differences in the blood of those who went on to have a cardiovascular event, such as a heart attack or stroke, more than a decade beforehand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Early warning signs could help doctors predict those at risk of a heart attack or stroke up to 30 years before an event, research suggests.

Scientists identified early patterns in a range of risk factors for cardiovascular disease – conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels – including high blood pressure, diabetes and kidney function.

They also revealed differences in the blood of those who went on to have a cardiovascular event, such as a heart attack or stroke, more than a decade beforehand.

The findings highlight a large window of opportunity to intervene to reduce cardiovascular risk and prevent the development of serious disease, experts say.

It has been revealed that cardiovascular disease kills one in four people in the UK. Traditional risk factors, such as high blood pressure and cholesterol, have been widely linked to the risk of disease. However, previous studies have typically focused on a single risk factor and don’t monitor long-term changes.

Other influences, such as kidney function and biomarkers in the blood, could also play an important role in establishing disease risk.

A research team, led by the University of Edinburgh, examined data from more than 100,000 people between 1985 and 2019 to explore the patterns of multiple risk factors in relation to cardiovascular events over time.

The research, funded by the British Heart Foundation, included data from four population studies across the United States, Norway and the United Kingdom.

Systolic blood pressure – the pressure in arteries when the heart beats or contracts – was consistently higher in those who went on to develop cardiovascular disease compared with those who were event-free, starting at 4 mmHg higher three decades before and increasing to 7 mmHg closer to the event.

Recent findings suggest that patterns were different between sexes throughout life. Younger women had lower blood pressure than younger men, but this switched around the age of 65, when female readings tended to be higher than males.

Recent findings suggest that researchers also identified key differences by age. Those who experienced a cardiovascular event at a younger age were more likely to have diabetes and a higher body mass index in the decades before the event.

Patterns in blood biomarkers also revealed early differences between those who went on to develop cardiovascular disease compared with those who didn’t. Changes in the levels of a protein called NT-proBNP – used to monitor heart failure – could be seen up to 10 years beforehand.

Trajectories of other non-traditional cardiovascular risk factors, including physical activity and kidney function, also differed between individuals with and without cardiovascular events.

In a recent development, tracking the course of risk factors over time may help to better predict serious cardiovascular events, experts say. Further research should also explore whether incorporating non-traditional risk factors could help to improve the estimation of cardiovascular disease risk, they add.

The study did not look at risk factors by ethnicity, and the team cautions that further research exploring potential differences in risk factor and biomarker trajectories across ethnic groups is needed.

I am excited about the findings of our study as they show that modifiable risk factors begin to diverge 30 years before a cardiovascular event occurs. This highlights a great opportunity to develop early prevention strategies throughout the life course, utilising the patterns of established and emerging risk factors and biomarkers to reduce future cardiovascular events.

For the vast majority of people, heart attacks and strokes are completely preventable. But many of us don’t realise we are at risk until it’s too late.

Sources indicate that this study adds to growing evidence that red flags for cardiovascular disease appear decades before it arrives. That could lead to a simple blood pressure reading, or proteins in the blood, being used to forewarn people of their future cardiovascular risk. Knowledge like this could empower people to make lifestyle changes or start treatment while they are still relatively young, which might reduce their risk, prevent a heart attack or stroke, and rewrite their future.

For now, it is worth remembering that we can all find out our risk of cardiovascular disease, for example by ‘knowing your numbers’ and getting your blood pressure and cholesterol checked, or having a free NHS health check with your GP in midlife for those living in England.

Nothing’s AI Earbuds Will Serve as an All-in-One Conversation Recorder

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, phone-maker Nothing Technology is breaking away from its typical retro-inspired designs with a new pair of AI-powered earbuds, as reported earlier by Bloomberg.
  • In a recent development, the Ear Note earbuds are designed primarily to maximize the recording functionality.
  • The earbuds can capture and transcribe phone calls, while the charging case has its own microphone to record in-person conversations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, phone-maker Nothing Technology is breaking away from its typical retro-inspired designs with a new pair of AI-powered earbuds, as reported earlier by Bloomberg. The manufacturer confirmed via an X post that its Ear Note wireless earbuds will be available starting Dec. 8.

In a recent development, the Ear Note earbuds are designed primarily to maximize the recording functionality. While other AI earbuds have already hit the market, the Ear Note is the first to record both phone calls and in-person conversations.

The earbuds can capture and transcribe phone calls, while the charging case has its own microphone to record in-person conversations. To mitigate privacy concerns, the case only records with a physical button press — a tell that could reveal when audio is being captured around the Ear Note user.

Nothing shared that the Ear Note will work with multiple popular AI agents, but the full list of compatible software has not yet been released. The Ear Note works in tandem with an app that stores recordings from the earbuds and case, creating transcriptions and summaries similar to those created by the popular Otter AI app.

The Nothing brand has developed a cult following for combining lifestyle and fashion trends in its suite of smartphones, headphones, speakers and watches.

The full product lineup is built with modern hardware, but mimics warm, nearly retrofuturist design sensibilities. The blocky Ear Note charging case continues this trend while taking the organization’s tech in a fresh direction.

In the lead-up to the Ear Note’s reveal, Nothing CEO Carl Pei described the earbuds in an X post as “a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product.”.

In a Bloomberg interview, Pei indicated that Nothing isn’t trying to create AI agents or software, but that the company has a “really interesting opportunity to be the hardware layer to AI.”.

It’s right now unclear how much the Ear Note earbuds and case will cost when they’re released next month. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the organization hasn’t settled on a price just yet. The most expensive earbuds currently available on the Nothing store cost $149.

Industry observers note that whether you’re covering your eyes, plugging your ears or slapping a timepiece on your wrist, there’s now an ever-present option to record the world around you. Multiple companies have created their own versions of smart glasses, earbuds and watches with augmented reality capabilities.

According to recent reports, now that AI is the flavor du jour, these existing features are being enhanced by newly introduced ways to scan and interact with the surrounding environment. That means a lot of visual and auditory data is being recorded by wearable devices, and very rarely with the consent of all parties involved.

The most immediate risk factors are associated with video recording – public distrust of smart glasses is so widespread that they’ve colloquially been coined “pervert glasses,” as folks fear they fundamentally break an unspoken social contract by obscuring public recording from other people.

But audio recording, enabled by Apple’s latest smartwatches, the Amazon Bee, Plaud earbuds and the latest Ear Note, is also raising concerns, not least because many states require all-party consent before you can record conversations.

The Ear Note’s ability to record every bit of audio, from phone calls to in-person conversations, means it will be handling more sensitive information than other AI-powered earbuds. The company will need to face new challenges to ensure security measures are in place to prevent private chats from leaking.

At the very least, it seems as though Nothing Technology is aware of these privacy risks. According to Bloomberg, the tech giant created a data and security team to address concerns that cropped up during the Ear Note’s development. The company has also “obtained the same privacy certifications as competing recording products and worked with law firms to assess potential risks and safeguards.”.

Pei called wearables with recording functionality a sensitive space, and said the design team was “extra careful to not take any risks.” The Ear Note earbuds and case are largely controlled by user commands, including tactile button presses that begin the recording process.
